question: A developer created a Lightning web component that uses a lightning-record-edit-form to collect information about Leads. Users complain that they only see one error message at a time about their input when trying to save a Lead record. What is the recommended approach to perform validations on more than one field, and display multiple error messages simultaneously with minimal JavaScript intervention?
optionA: Try/catch/finally block
optionB: External JavaScript library
optionC: Validation rules
optionD: Apex trigger
explanation:
Validation rules are what Salesforce recommends, and the lightning-record-edit-form documentation says so in as many words: "We recommend using custom validation rules to verify data input instead of implementing client-side validation errors." A single validation rule's formula can evaluate the data in one or more fields, so the multi-field checking this question asks for is expressed declaratively with no JavaScript at all — and because the rule lives on the object, it protects every entry point into the data, not just this component.
One correction to the question's premise, because it is a common misconception: this form does not display several errors at once. Its documentation states that if a single field has multiple validation errors the form shows only the first error on that field, and that if a submitted form has multiple errors it shows only the first error encountered, revealing the next as each is corrected. The "displays all error messages at once" behaviour described in Validation Rule Considerations applies to the standard page-layout UI, not to lightning-record-edit-form. Validation rules are the right answer here because they are the recommended, declarative, multi-field mechanism — not because they change how many messages the component renders.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (try/catch/finally block) — reacts to an error that has already been thrown; it validates nothing.
Option B (external JavaScript library) — the client-side route the documentation explicitly steers you away from, and the opposite of "minimal JavaScript intervention".
Option D (Apex trigger) — addError() could enforce the same rules, but it is code where configuration already does the job.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/lightning-component-reference/guide/lightning-record-edit-form.html
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.fields_validation_considerations.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: Answer C stands, and is now cited to the sentence that actually settles it: the lightning-record-edit-form guide recommends custom validation rules over client-side validation errors. The explanation was wrong on mechanism, though — it claimed validation rules "display multiple error messages at once on lightning-record-edit-form", and the component's own documentation says the opposite, that a submitted form with multiple errors shows only the first error encountered. The "all messages at once" rule in Validation Rule Considerations describes the standard page-layout UI and was misapplied here.

question: Consider the queries below with this information: More than 200,000 Account records, records include soft-deleted records (in Recycle Bin), and two fields marked as External Id: Customer_Number__c and ERP_Key__c. Which two queries are optimized for large data volumes? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: SELECT Id FROM Account WHERE Name != NULL
optionB: SELECT Id FROM Account WHERE Name != '' AND Customer_Number__c = 'ValueA'
optionC: SELECT Id FROM Account WHERE Id IN :aListVariable
optionD: SELECT Id FROM Account WHERE Name != '' AND IsDeleted = false
explanation:
The query filtering on Customer_Number__c and the query filtering on Id are the two optimized ones. Customer_Number__c is marked as an External ID, and Salesforce creates an index on any External ID field, so an equality filter on it is selective. Id is the primary key, which is always indexed; binding a bounded list of Ids keeps the filter selective. Selectivity comes from filtering on an indexed field with a narrow result set, not from restating a default.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (WHERE Name != NULL) — matches essentially every row, so the optimizer falls back to a full table scan.
Option D (WHERE Name != '' AND IsDeleted = false) — Name != '' matches nearly every record, and IsDeleted = false adds nothing the optimizer can use, because a SOQL query already excludes soft-deleted rows unless you add ALL ROWS.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_infrastructure_indexes.htm

corrected.note: Key B,C is right, but the explanation argued for B and D — it defended an option the key does not name. The LDV Indexes page settles it: External IDs cause an index to be created on that field, and the record Id is the primary key index.

optionC: @testSetup method to set up expected data

explanation:
Test.setFixedSearchResults() is the fix. SOSL behaves differently under test than it does at runtime: the Apex Developer Guide states that to keep test methods predictable, any SOSL query in an Apex test returns an empty set of search results — so searchTestAccounts() returns nothing, accounts.size() is 0, and the assertion fails no matter how many matching Accounts the test inserted first. Test.setFixedSearchResults() defines the list of record ids the search should return for the remainder of the test, so the method under test receives the Account the test created.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (@isTest(SeeAllData=true)) — widens which records a query can see, but it does not switch SOSL back on in a test.
Option C (@testSetup method) — a way of creating test data, and creating more data doesn't help when the search is returning an empty list by design.
Option D (Test.loadData) — the same problem: it loads records, and the search still returns nothing.

question: Which technique can run custom logic when a Lightning web component is loaded?
optionA: Use an <aura:handler> init event to call a function
optionB: Use the rendered() callback method
optionC: Call $A.enqueueAction and pass in the method to call
optionD: Use the connectedCallback() method
explanation:
The connectedCallback() lifecycle hook is the LWC method that runs when a component is inserted into the DOM, which is what "when the component is loaded" means in a Lightning web component. It fires on the component and again on each re-insertion, so it is the documented place for initialisation logic.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (<aura:handler> init event) — Aura syntax; a Lightning web component has no aura:handler.
Option B (rendered() callback) — no such hook exists in LWC; the render-phase hook is renderedCallback(), and even that fires after every render rather than once on load.
Option C ($A.enqueueAction) — the Aura framework's server-action queue; $A does not exist in LWC.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/lwc/guide/create-lifecycle-hooks-dom.html

question: A company has a native iOS order placement app that needs to connect to Salesforce to retrieve consolidated information from many different objects in a JSON format. Which is the optimal method to implement this in Salesforce?
optionA: Apex REST web service
optionB: Apex SOAP web service
optionC: Apex SOAP callout
optionD: Apex REST callout
explanation:
An Apex REST web service is the optimal method: it creates a custom endpoint in Salesforce that an external system such as the iOS app can call, returns JSON natively, and can consolidate data from many objects into a single response shaped for the caller. The direction matters here — the app is calling into Salesforce, so Salesforce must expose a service, not make a callout.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Apex SOAP web service) — also exposes Salesforce as a provider, but SOAP is XML-based; JSON is the format the app needs.
Option C (Apex SOAP callout) — a callout is Salesforce calling an external system, the reverse of this flow.
Option D (Apex REST callout) — the same direction problem: outbound from Salesforce, when the app needs to call in.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_rest.htm

question:
Requirements:
1) For mobile devices, information should display in three rows.
2) For desktops and tablets, information should display in a single row.
Which option has the correct component code to meet the requirements for desktops and tablets?
optionA: Set size='12' medium-device-size='4'
optionB: Set size='12' medium-device-size='6' large-device-size='4'
optionC: Set size='12' large-device-size='4'
optionD: Set size='12' medium-device-size='6'
explanation:
size='12' with medium-device-size='4' is the setting. lightning-layout is a mobile-first 12-column grid: size sets the width at the smallest breakpoint and applies upward until a device-specific attribute overrides it, and the device attributes are additive — small-device-size means a phone, medium-device-size a tablet, large-device-size a desktop, and each applies to the size named and everything larger.
Three items at size='12' each take the full width, so on a phone they stack into three rows — the first requirement. To place all three on a single row from tablet upward, each has to occupy a third of the grid at the medium breakpoint, which is medium-device-size='4'.
One thing worth fixing in your mental model: size='12' never produces a single row on any device. Full width means one item per row everywhere, including desktop.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (medium-device-size='6' large-device-size='4') — repairs the desktop but leaves the tablet at two per row, and the requirement names tablets explicitly.
Option C (large-device-size='4' only) — tablets inherit size='12', so they keep the three-row phone layout.
Option D (medium-device-size='6') — half width, so a tablet shows two items on the first row and the third below it, and that stays true on desktop because the medium setting carries upward.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/lightning-component-reference/guide/lightning-layout-item.html
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/lightning-component-reference/guide/lightning-layout.html

question: A Salesforce org has more than 50,000 contacts. A new business process requires a calculation that aggregates data from all contact records. This calculation needs to run once a day after business hours. Which two steps should a developer take? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Queueable interface
optionB: Implement Database.Batchable interface
optionC: Implement Schedulable interface
optionD: @future annotation
explanation:
Implementing Database.Batchable and implementing Schedulable are the two steps, and they are doing different jobs. Database.Batchable carries the volume; Schedulable supplies the recurrence. The Schedulable class's execute() calls Database.executeBatch() on the Batchable class, and System.schedule() sets it to run after hours.
Batch Apex escapes the 50,000-row query limit by a documented mechanism rather than by being bigger: if start() returns a Database.QueryLocator, the governor limit for the total number of records retrieved by SOQL queries is bypassed, and a QueryLocator can cover up to 50 million records. Separately, each execute() chunk is a discrete transaction whose governor limits are reset, which is what gives the processing room. Those are two different guarantees, and only Batch Apex offers either. The Apex Scheduler documentation names the pairing directly: it is "ideal for daily or weekly maintenance tasks using Batch Apex".
One detail that catches people out: scheduled Apex is asynchronous, but synchronous governor limits apply to a scheduled job. Schedulable on its own therefore buys no headroom, which is exactly why the Batchable half of this answer is required and not merely tidier.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Queueable interface) — a single transaction with a single set of governor limits; the 50,000-row SOQL limit is the same in asynchronous Apex, so selecting every Contact fails outright, and its only timing control is a 0–10 minute enqueue delay with no recurrence and no time of day.
Option D (@future annotation) — can't be scheduled, returns no job id, can't be chained, and accepts only primitives; the 50 usually quoted alongside it is the maximum number of future methods per Apex invocation, not a cap on records per call.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_batch_interface.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_scheduler.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_queueing_jobs.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_gov_limits.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_classes_annotation_future.htm

question: Universal Containers wants to notify an external system when an unhandled exception occurs in their nightly Apex batch job. What is the appropriate publish/subscribe logic?
optionA: Have the external system subscribe to a custom Platform Event that gets fired with addError()
optionB: Have the external system subscribe to a custom Platform Event that gets fired with EventBus.publish()
optionC: Have the external system subscribe to a standard Platform Event that gets fired with EventBus.publish()
optionD: Have the external system subscribe to a standard Platform Event that gets fired
explanation:
A standard Platform Event that gets fired by the platform is the answer, and its name is BatchApexErrorEvent. The Apex Developer Guide states that if the start, execute, or finish method of a batch Apex job encounters an unhandled exception, a BatchApexErrorEvent is fired, and that to get this behaviour the batch class declaration must implement the Database.RaisesPlatformEvents marker interface. The event's own reference page then settles the rest of the option set in a single line: "Only the Salesforce Platform can fire this event; Apex code and the API can't."
The same page lists the supported subscribers as Apex triggers, flows, processes, the Pub/Sub API, and the Streaming API (CometD), so an external system genuinely can listen on the /event/BatchApexErrorEvent channel. It receives the AsyncApexJob id, the exception type and message, the stack trace, and the record ids that were in scope at the time of failure.
There is also a reason no custom-event design could have worked here. An unhandled exception is by definition not caught, so there is no point in your own code at which to publish, and an event published with the default publish-after-commit behaviour is discarded when the transaction rolls back.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (custom Platform Event fired with addError()) — addError() adds a record-level error inside a trigger and publishes nothing at all.
Option B (custom Platform Event fired with EventBus.publish()) — there is no point in your code at which to publish an unhandled exception, and the publish would roll back with the transaction anyway.
Option C (standard Platform Event fired with EventBus.publish()) — Apex code can't fire BatchApexErrorEvent; only the platform can.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_batch_platformevents.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.platform_events.meta/platform_events/sforce_api_objects_batchapexerrorevent.htm

corrected.note: The Apex Developer Guide documents BatchApexErrorEvent as a standard platform event fired automatically by the platform for unhandled batch exceptions, gated only on implementing Database.RaisesPlatformEvents. No custom event and no EventBus.publish() call is involved, which is what the old key B asserted.

question: After a platform event is defined in a Salesforce org, events can be published via which mechanism?
optionA: External Apps use an API to publish event messages
optionB: Internal Apps can use entitlement processes
optionC: External Apps require the standard Streaming API
optionD: Internal Apps can use outbound messages
explanation:
External apps using an API to publish event messages is the supported mechanism. Once a platform event is defined, an external application publishes it through the REST API (a POST to the sobjects endpoint for the event), the SOAP API, or the Pub/Sub API, exactly as it would create a record.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (entitlement processes) — a Service Cloud feature for service contracts and milestones; it has nothing to do with the event bus.
Option C (the standard Streaming API) — the Streaming API subscribes to events; it cannot publish them.
Option D (outbound messages) — send data from Salesforce to an external endpoint over SOAP; they neither publish nor consume platform events.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.platform_events.meta/platform_events/platform_events_publish.htm

question: A multi-national company needs a Lightning application that respects user's locale context for dates, times, numbers, currency, and currency symbols. When using Aura components, which approach should the developer implement?
optionA: Use the $User global variable to retrieve user preferences
optionB: Use the $Label global value provider
optionC: Use the $Locale value provider to retrieve user preferences
optionD: Create a Hierarchical custom setting to store user preferences
explanation:
The $Locale value provider is the approach. It exposes the user's locale-derived settings — date, time and number formats, currency code and symbol, decimal and grouping separators, time zone — so an Aura component can format values the way the running user expects without storing anything itself.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A ($User global variable) — a Visualforce and formula global, not an Aura value provider; Aura's are $Browser, $Label, $Locale, $Resource and $SObjectType, and user record fields hold no formatting logic anyway.
Option B ($Label global value provider) — retrieves custom labels for translated text; it says nothing about how to format a date or a currency.
Option D (hierarchical custom setting) — would require you to build and maintain the locale data by hand that the platform already provides.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.lightning.meta/lightning/expr_locale_value_provider.htm

question: A developer has three savepoints SP1, SP2, SP3 (created in order). During execution, code rolls back to SP1, fixes a condition, then tries to roll back to SP3, causing a runtime error. Why?
optionA: SP3 became invalid when SP1 was rolled back
optionB: The developer has too many DML statements between savepoints
optionC: The developer used too many savepoints in one trigger session
optionD: The developer should have called SP2 before calling SP3
explanation:
SP3 became invalid when SP1 was rolled back. Rolling back to an earlier savepoint invalidates every savepoint created after it, so the rollback to SP1 discards SP2 and SP3 together. A later rollback to SP3 therefore refers to a savepoint that no longer exists, and the runtime raises an error.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (too many DML statements between savepoints) — there is no such rule; DML between savepoints is what a savepoint exists to bracket.
Option C (too many savepoints in one trigger session) — savepoints and rollbacks count against the DML statement limit, but three is nowhere near it, and the error would be a limit exception rather than an invalid-savepoint error.
Option D (should have called SP2 first) — rolling back to SP2 would fail for the same reason: it was invalidated along with SP3.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/langCon_apex_transaction_control.htm

question: Assuming the CreateOneAccount class implements the Queueable interface, which syntax properly tests the Apex code?
explanation:
Test.startTest(); System.enqueueJob(); Test.stopTest(); then the query and assertion is the syntax. A queueable job is asynchronous, so nothing it does is visible to the test until the platform is told to drain the queue. Enclosing System.enqueueJob() in Test.startTest() and Test.stopTest() is what forces that: every asynchronous process started inside the block runs synchronously when Test.stopTest() is reached, so an assertion placed after it sees the job's results.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (no start/stop block) — the job is still sitting in the queue when the query runs, so the assertion tests the state of the org before the job ever executed.
Option C (assertion before Test.stopTest()) — it is the stopTest() call that drains the queue, not startTest(), so an assertion above it is still running too early.
Option D (Database.executeBatch()) — the entry point for a class implementing Database.Batchable; handing it a Queueable does not compile, because the two interfaces are unrelated.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_queueing_jobs.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_testing_tools_start_stop_test.htm

question: When developing a Lightning web component, which setting displays lightning-layout-items in one column on small devices and two columns on tablet/desktop screens?
optionA: Set size='12' tablet-device-size='6'
optionB: Set size='12' medium-device-size='6'
optionC: Set size='6' mobile-device-size='12'
optionD: Set size='6' small-device-size='12'
explanation:
size='12' with medium-device-size='6' is the setting. lightning-layout is a 12-column grid: size sets the base width at the small breakpoint, so size='12' gives full width on a phone — one column — and medium-device-size='6' gives half width from tablet upward, which is two columns on tablet and desktop.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (tablet-device-size='6') — no such attribute; the breakpoints are small, medium and large.
Option C (size='6' mobile-device-size='12') — no mobile-device-size attribute exists, and size='6' would put two columns on the smallest screens.
Option D (size='6' small-device-size='12') — small-device-size applies to phones and upward, so it would override the size='6' everywhere and give one column on every device.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/lightning-component-reference/guide/lightning-layout-item.html

question: Which interface needs to be implemented by an Aura component so it may be displayed in modal dialog by clicking a button on a Lightning record page?
optionA: force:lightningEditAction
optionB: lightning:editAction
optionC: force:lightningQuickAction
optionD: lightning:quickAction
explanation:
force:lightningQuickAction is the interface. An Aura component that implements it can be used as a Lightning quick action, and the record-page button then opens the component in a modal dialog with the standard header and Cancel control.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (force:lightningEditAction) — not an Aura interface.
Option B (lightning:editAction) — not an Aura interface either.
Option D (lightning:quickAction) — the interfaces for quick actions are in the force namespace; lightning:quickAction does not exist.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.lightning.meta/lightning/components_using_lex_s1_config_action.htm

question: A developer creates a Lightning web component for Contact entry, but error messages are not displayed. Which component should be added to display error messages?
optionA: apex:messages
optionB: lightning-messages
optionC: lightning-error
optionD: aura:messages
explanation:
lightning-messages is the component to add. Inside a lightning-record-edit-form it automatically displays the errors generated when lightning-input-field values are processed, so a form that has no lightning-messages shows nothing when a save fails.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (apex:messages) — Visualforce syntax; it cannot be used in a Lightning web component.
Option C (lightning-error) — no such base component exists.
Option D (aura:messages) — Aura syntax, and not a real Aura component either.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/lightning-component-reference/guide/lightning-record-edit-form.html

question:
A Visualforce page contains an industry select list and displays a table of Accounts that have a matching value in their Industry field.
<apex:selectList value="{!selectedIndustry}">
<apex:selectOptions values="{!industries}"/>
</apex:selectList>
When a user changes the value in the industry select list, the table of Accounts should be automatically updated to show the Accounts associated with the selected industry.
What is the optimal way to implement this?
optionA: Add an <apex:actionFunction> within the <apex:selectOptions>.
optionB: Add an <apex:actionFunction> within the <apex:selectList>.
optionC: Add an <apex:actionSupport> within the <apex:selectList>.
optionD: Add an <apex:actionSupport> within the <apex:selectOptions>.
explanation:
An <apex:actionSupport> within the <apex:selectList> is the optimal implementation. actionSupport attaches AJAX behaviour to an existing component's browser event — here onchange on the select list — and calls the controller action and re-renders the Account table without a full page refresh and without any JavaScript of your own.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (<apex:actionFunction> within <apex:selectOptions>) — actionFunction defines a JavaScript function you must call yourself, and selectOptions is not an interactive component.
Option B (<apex:actionFunction> within <apex:selectList>) — still needs an onchange handler written in JavaScript to invoke it, so it is not the minimal route.
Option D (<apex:actionSupport> within <apex:selectOptions>) — selectOptions only supplies the option values; the change event belongs to the selectList.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.pages.meta/pages/pages_compref_actionSupport.htm

question: A company needs to automatically delete sensitive information after seven years. This could delete almost a million records daily. How can this be achieved?
optionA: Schedule an @future process with recursive 1000-record batches
optionB: Use aggregate functions to delete aggregateResults objects
optionC: Schedule a batch Apex process to run daily
optionD: Perform a SOSL statement and delete the entire result set
explanation:
Scheduling a batch Apex process to run daily is how this is achieved. Batch Apex is designed for large volumes: a QueryLocator can cover up to 50 million records, and each execute() chunk is its own transaction with its own governor limits, so almost a million deletions a day is within reach. Implementing Schedulable, or scheduling from Setup, gives the daily cadence.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (@future with recursive 1,000-record batches) — a future method cannot call another future method, so it cannot chain, and it has no scheduling mechanism.
Option B (aggregate functions to delete AggregateResult objects) — AggregateResult rows are query output, not records; they cannot be deleted.
Option D (SOSL and delete the entire result set) — SOSL returns at most 2,000 records per query and is a search, not a deletion mechanism.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_batch_interface.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_scheduler.htm

question:
A company's support process dictates that any time a Case is closed with a Status of 'Could not fix', an Engineering Review custom object record should be created and populated with information from the Case, the Contact, and any of the Products associated with the Case.
What is the correct way to automate this using an Apex trigger?
optionA: An after update trigger that creates the Engineering Review record and inserts it
optionB: A before update trigger that creates the Engineering Review record and inserts it
optionC: An after upsert trigger that creates the Engineering Review record and inserts it
optionD: A before upsert trigger that creates the Engineering Review record and inserts it
explanation:
An after update trigger that creates the Engineering Review record and inserts it is the correct automation. The Engineering Review needs data from the Case, its Contact and its Products, and it should be created only once the Case has actually been saved with the closing status — an after trigger runs once the record has been validated and written, so Trigger.new carries the committed values and the related record can be inserted with a real Case id to reference.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (before update trigger) — runs before the Case is saved, so the status change may still fail validation; before triggers are for modifying the record itself, not for creating related records.
Option C (after upsert trigger) — upsert is not a trigger event; the events are insert, update, delete and undelete.
Option D (before upsert trigger) — the same non-existent event, and in the before phase besides.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_triggers_context_variables.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_triggers.htm

question: An Apex trigger creates an order record when an Opportunity is won, but recently it's creating two orders. What is the optimal troubleshooting technique?
optionA: Disable all flows and re-enable one at a time
optionB: Run Apex Test Classes to ensure code coverage
optionC: Set up debug logging for every Sales Rep
optionD: Add system.debug() statements and use Developer Console logs
explanation:
Adding System.debug() statements and reading the Developer Console logs is the optimal technique. The log shows every time the trigger fires, in what order, and which other automation ran in the same transaction — so a duplicate order shows up either as the trigger executing twice (a recursion or a re-fire after a workflow field update) or as a second piece of automation doing the same work.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (disable all flows and re-enable one at a time) — a blind bisection in what is presumably production; the log shows the same thing in one run without turning anything off.
Option B (run Apex test classes for coverage) — coverage measures which lines execute, not how many times a trigger fires in a real transaction.
Option C (debug logging for every Sales Rep) — floods the log store with noise; one trace flag on one reproducing user is enough.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_debugging_debug_log.htm

question:
A developer created a Lightning web component that uses a Lightning_record_edit_fom to collect Information about Leads. Users complain that they only see one error message at a time about their input when trying to save a Lead record.
Which best practice should the developer use to perform the validations on more than one held, thus allowing more than one error message to be displayed simultaneously?
optionA: Apex REST
optionB: Client_side validation
optionC: Custom validation rules
optionD: Next Best Action
explanation:
Custom validation rules are the documented recommendation, and the lightning-record-edit-form guide states the comparison this question is built on directly: "We recommend using custom validation rules to verify data input instead of implementing client-side validation errors." A validation rule's formula can evaluate the data in one or more fields, which is the multi-field validation the question asks for, and it is enforced on the object — so it holds for the API, Data Loader, flows and every other UI, not only for this component.
Be careful with the premise, though. Reaching for validation rules will not, on its own, produce several error messages side by side. The component's documentation states that if a single field has multiple validation errors the form shows only the first error on that field, and that if a submitted form has multiple errors it shows only the first error encountered, showing the next one as each is corrected. The "displays all error messages at once" statement in Validation Rule Considerations describes the standard page-layout UI. If the requirement is genuinely to surface several problems in one pass, the honest answer is to write one rule whose formula covers the related fields and whose message names them together.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Apex REST) — an inbound integration mechanism; it does not validate form input.
Option B (client-side validation) — reimplements business rules in JavaScript, protects one entry point, and is what the guide tells you not to do.
Option D (Next Best Action) — serves recommendations; it validates nothing.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/lightning-component-reference/guide/lightning-record-edit-form.html
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.fields_validation_considerations.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: Answer C stands; two separate defects fixed. First, as originally scraped the explanation was self-contradictory — it declared "Option B (Client-side validation) is correct" while the key names C, and then listed C among the options that are "not directly related". The lightning-record-edit-form guide settles that head-to-head explicitly in favour of validation rules. Second, the replacement text written in the first pass justified C by claiming the form displays all failing validation messages at once; the component's documentation states the opposite, that it shows only the first error encountered. That claim came from Validation Rule Considerations, which describes the standard page-layout UI, and has been removed rather than restated.

question:
Universal Containers uses a custom Lightning page to provide a mechanism to perform a step-by-step wizard search for Accounts. One of the steps in the wizard is to allow the user to input text into a text field, ERF Number_c, that is then used in a query to find matching Accounts. 
erpNumber = + '%';
List<Account> accounts = [SELECT Id,Name FROM Account WHERE ERP_Number__c LIKE :erpNumber]
The query needs to be optimized. Which option would be best?
optionA: Perform the SOQL query as part of a for loop.
optionB: Mark the ERP_Numker = field as an external Id
optionC: Mark the ERP_Number__ c field as required.
optionD: Move the SO0L query to within an asynchronous process.
explanation:
Marking the ERP_Number__c field as an External ID is the best option. An External ID field is automatically indexed, so the query can use the index to locate matching Accounts instead of scanning the whole table. A LIKE filter with a trailing wildcard ('value%') can still use that index; only a leading wildcard defeats it.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (SOQL inside a for loop) — repeats the query per iteration, which is the governor-limit anti-pattern and makes nothing faster.
Option C (mark the field as required) — required affects data entry, not query planning; it creates no index.
Option D (move the query into an asynchronous process) — the query costs the same in async; the slowness is moved, not removed.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_infrastructure_indexes.htm

question:
A company has a Lightning page with many Lightning Components, some that cache reference data. It is reported that the page does not always show the most current reference data.
What can a developer use to analyze and diagnose the problem in the Lightning page?
optionA: Salesforce Lightning Inspector Actions Tab
optionB: Salesforce Lightning Inspector Event Log Tab
optionC: Salesforce Lightning Inspector Transactions Tab
optionD: Salesforce Lightning Inspector Storage Tab
explanation:
The Salesforce Lightning Inspector Storage tab is the tool. It shows the client-side cache Lightning components use — storable actions and Lightning Data Service — so you can see which reference data is cached, when it was stored and when it expires, which is exactly what you need when the symptom is stale cached data.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Actions tab) — lists server actions and their parameters and responses, not what is held in the cache.
Option B (Event Log tab) — traces component and application events as they fire.
Option C (Transactions tab) — performance timings for the page's transactions; it says nothing about cache contents.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/developer-relations/2016/02/introducing-salesforce-lightning-inspector
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.lightning.meta/lightning/controllers_server_storable_actions.htm

optionA: Use a Map accountMap instead of List accountList.
optionB: Move the Region__c query to outside the loop.
optionC: Use a Map to cache the results of the Region__c query by Id.
optionD: Remove the last line updating accountList as it is not needed.
explanation:
Moving the Region__c query outside the loop and removing the trailing update accountList are the two changes, and both defects are visible inside the loop.
The Region__c query runs once per Account in Trigger.new. A bulk update of 200 Accounts issues 200 queries and the transaction dies on the 101st. Move it out: query the regions once for every Region_Name__c in the batch, build a Map<String, Region__c> keyed by Name, and look each Account's region up from that map inside the loop.
The trailing update accountList is not merely unnecessary — it is not allowed. accountList holds the same sObjects as Trigger.new, and the Apex Developer Guide states plainly that trigger.new and trigger.old cannot be used in Apex DML operations. In a before trigger you don't need it anyway: "You can use an object to change its own field values using trigger.new, but only in before triggers", and those assignments are saved when the trigger finishes.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Map accountMap instead of List accountList) — alters neither defect; the collection type was never the problem.
Option C (cache the query results in a Map keyed by Id) — the lookup here is by Region Name rather than by Id, and on its own it still leaves the query inside the loop.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_triggers_bulk.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_triggers_bulk_idioms.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_triggers_context_variables_considerations.htm

As scraped the trigger body was corrupted — a mangled SELECT clause, a missing object name, and the OwnerId assignment and add() call shown outside the loop — and optionA was an empty string, so a four-option question presented three. The stem has been replaced with the intact trigger and the missing fourth option restored, keeping the existing lettering so the key still resolves to "move the query outside the loop" and "remove the update". The reason for removing the update is now cited to the documented rule that trigger.new cannot be used in DML operations, rather than to it merely being redundant.

question:
Universal Containers wants to use a Customer Community with Customer Community Plus licenses so their customers can track how many containers they are renting and when they are due back. Many of their customers are global companies with complex Account hierarchies, representing various departments within the same organization. One of the requirements is that certain community users within the same Account hierarchy be able to see several departments' containers, based on a junction object that relates the Contact to the various Account records that represent the departments.
Which solution solves these requirements?
optionA: A Visualforce page that uses a custom controller that specifies without sharing expose the records
optionB: An Apex trigger that creates Apex managed sharing records based on the junction object's relationships
optionC: A Lightning web component on the Community Home Page that uses Lightning Data Services.
optionD: A custom list view on the junction object with filters that will show the proper records based on owner
explanation:
An Apex trigger that creates Apex managed sharing records based on the junction object's relationships is the solution. Community Plus users get record access through sharing, and the rule here — a Contact may see the containers of several departmental Accounts, as defined by junction records — is data-driven in a way neither the role hierarchy nor a criteria-based sharing rule can express. A trigger on the junction object that inserts and deletes share records as relationships change is what Apex managed sharing exists for.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Visualforce page with a without sharing controller) — bypasses sharing for everyone who reaches the page, exposing every department's records rather than the ones the junction object grants.
Option C (Lightning web component using Lightning Data Service) — LDS respects the user's sharing, so it can only show what the user can already see; it grants nothing.
Option D (custom list view filtered by owner) — a list view can only show records the user already has access to, and ownership is not the relationship the requirement describes.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_bulk_sharing_creating_with_apex.htm

optionB:
SELECT AccountId, CreatedDate, Subject 
FROM Task 
WHERE CreatedDate >= :startDate AND CreatedDate <= :endDate 
AND IsDeleted = false;
optionC:
SELECT AccountId, CreatedDate, Subject 
FROM Task 
WHERE CreatedDate >= :startDate AND CreatedDate <= :endDate 
ALL ROWS;
optionD:
SELECT AccountId, CreatedDate, Subject 
FROM Task 
WHERE CreatedDate >= :startDate AND CreatedDate <= :endDate 
AND IsDeleted = false 
ALL ROWS;
explanation:
The query with both IsDeleted = false and ALL ROWS is the valid one. ALL ROWS tells SOQL to return records that are normally hidden — both those in the Recycle Bin and archived activities — and the requirement says to include archived Tasks; the IsDeleted = false filter then removes the Recycle Bin rows that ALL ROWS would otherwise let through. The date range on CreatedDate between the two bind variables covers 12 to 24 months old.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (date range only) — without ALL ROWS, archived Tasks are excluded, and Tasks are archived automatically once they are old enough.
Option B (IsDeleted = false without ALL ROWS) — the filter is redundant on a normal query, which already excludes deleted rows, and archived Tasks are still missing.
Option C (ALL ROWS without IsDeleted = false) — includes archived Tasks but also returns the deleted ones the requirement says to exclude.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/langCon_apex_SOQL_query_all_rows.htm

question:
A developer is tasked with creating a Lightning web component that allows users to create a Case for a selected product, directly from a custom Lightning page. The input fields in the component are displayed in a non-linear fashion on top of an image of the product to help the user better understand the meaning of the fields.
Which two components should a developer use to implement the creation of the Case from the Lightning web component?
Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Lightning-record-edit-form
optionB: lightning-input-field
optionC: Lightning-input
optionD: lightning-record-form
explanation:
lightning-record-edit-form with lightning-input-field is the pair. lightning-record-edit-form handles the record creation through Lightning Data Service — field-level security, validation and the save itself — while each lightning-input-field is an individually placeable, record-bound input, so the fields can sit wherever the layout needs them, including scattered across an image.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option C (lightning-input) — a plain input with no binding to a record field; you would have to collect the values and write the record yourself.
Option D (lightning-record-form) — renders the fields in a fixed auto, full or compact layout, so the non-linear positioning the requirement asks for is not possible.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/lightning-component-reference/guide/lightning-record-edit-form.html
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/lwc/guide/data-create-record.html

question: What are three reasons that a developer should write Jest tests for Lightning web components? 3 options.
optionA: To test a component's non-public properties.
optionB: To test basic user interaction
optionC: To verify the DOM output of a component
optionD: To test how multiple components work together
optionE: To verify that events fire when expected
explanation:
Testing basic user interaction, verifying the DOM output of a component, and verifying that events fire when expected are the three reasons, and they are the ones the LWC testing guide lists almost verbatim: "Test basic user interaction (clicks)", "Verify the DOM output of a component", and "Verify that events fire when expected".
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (test a component's non-public properties) — Jest tests exercise a component's public API, its @api properties and methods and the events it fires; private state is an implementation detail.
Option D (test how multiple components work together) — Jest tests a component in isolation; integration between components is what end-to-end tools are for.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/lwc/guide/testing.html
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/lwc/guide/unit-testing-using-jest-create-tests.html

question:
A Visualforce page loads slowly due to the large amount of data it displays.
Which strategy can a developer use to improve the performance?
optionA: Use Javascript to move data processing to the browser instead of the controller.
optionB: Use the transient keywords for the List variables used in the custom controller.
optionC: Use lazy loading to load the data on demand, instead of the controller's constructor.
optionD: Use an <apex:actionPoller> in the page to load all of the data asynchronously.
explanation:
Lazy loading, so data is fetched on demand rather than in the controller's constructor, is the strategy. The constructor runs on every page load, so everything it queries is paid for whether or not the user ever looks at it; deferring each block of data until an action or scroll asks for it is what shrinks the initial load.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (move processing to the browser) — the data still has to be queried and sent; the query load is unchanged.
Option B (transient keyword on the lists) — shrinks view state, so it helps postbacks, but the data is still fetched on the first load.
Option D (apex:actionPoller) — polls the server repeatedly on a timer; it loads nothing on demand and adds requests rather than removing them.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.pages.meta/pages/pages_best_practices_perf_lazy_load.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_visualforce_best_practices.meta/salesforce_visualforce_best_practices/pages_best_practices_perf_code_view_state.htm

question:
Universal Containers wants to use an external Web Service provided by a third-party vendor to validate that shipping and billing addresses are correct. The current vendor uses basic password authentication, but Universal Containers might switch to a different vendor who uses OAuth.
What would allow Universal Containers to switch vendors without updating the code to handle authentication?
optionA: Custom Metadata
optionB: Custom Setting (List)
optionC: Dynamic Endpoint
optionD: Named Credential
explanation:
A Named Credential is what lets the vendor change without a code change. It packages the endpoint URL and the authentication in one Setup record; the Apex callout refers to it as callout:Vendor_Name and Salesforce injects the credentials at runtime. Switching from basic password authentication to OAuth is then a change to the named credential's authentication settings, and the callout code is untouched.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (custom metadata) — can hold the endpoint, but the code would still have to read the record and perform the authentication itself, so the OAuth change is a code change.
Option B (list custom setting) — the same problem, in a less deployable container.
Option C (dynamic endpoint) — changes where the callout goes, not how it authenticates.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?language=en_US&id=sf.named_credentials_about.htm&type=5

optionA: Remove the Database.setSavepoint and Database.rollback.
optionB: Change the CalloutUtil.makeRestCallout to an @InvocableMethod method.
optionC: Change the CalloutUtil.makeRestCallout to an @future method.
optionD: Move the CalloutUtil.makeRestCallout method call below the catch block.
explanation:
Changing CalloutUtil.makeRestCallout to an @future method is the fix. Apex forbids a callout in a transaction that has uncommitted DML — the inserts of the Requests and Request Lines are pending when the callout runs, which is exactly the error text. A future method runs in its own transaction after the current one commits, so the callout happens with no pending work; mark it @future(callout=true) and pass the ids, since a future method takes only primitives and collections of primitives.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (remove the savepoint and rollback) — the savepoint is not the problem; the pending inserts are, and they remain pending.
Option B (@InvocableMethod) — exposes the method to flows and does nothing to move it out of the transaction.
Option D (move the call below the catch block) — still the same transaction with the same uncommitted inserts, so the same error.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_callouts_timeouts.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_classes_annotation_future.htm

optionA: Add Test.startTest() before and Test.setMock and Test.stopTest() after CalloutUtil.sendAccountUpdate.
optionB: Add Test.startTest() and Test.setMock before and Test.stopTest() after CalloutUtil.sendAccountUpdate.
optionC: Add if (!Test.isRunningTest()) around CalloutUtil.sendAccountUpdate.
optionD: Add Test.startTest() before and Test.stopTest() after CalloutUtil.sendAccountUpdate.
explanation:
Test.startTest() and Test.setMock before the call, and Test.stopTest() after it, is the optimal fix. Apex tests cannot make real callouts; Test.setMock registers an HttpCalloutMock (or WebServiceMock) implementation so the callout returns a canned response instead. It has to be registered before CalloutUtil.sendAccountUpdate runs — a mock set after the call is set too late — and wrapping the call in startTest/stopTest keeps the setup DML separate from the code under test.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Test.setMock after the call) — the callout has already been attempted, unmocked, by the time the mock is registered, so the same error fires.
Option C (skip the callout when Test.isRunningTest()) — hides the callout from every test, leaves the code uncovered, and the assertion then checks a field nothing has updated.
Option D (startTest/stopTest with no mock) — the callout still runs for real, which is what the error is about.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_classes_restful_http_testing_httpcalloutmock.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_classes_restful_http_testing.htm

question:
A developer created and tested a Visualforce page in their developer sandbox, but now receives reports that users are encountering ViewState errors when using it in Production.
What should the developer ensure to correct these errors?
optionA: Ensure queries do not exceed governor limits.
optionB: Ensure properties are marked as Transient.
optionC: Ensure properties are marked as private.
optionD: Ensure profiles have access to the Visualforce page.
explanation:
Ensuring properties are marked as Transient is the correction. View state carries the page's controller state between server round trips and is limited to 170 KB; large collections, query results held for convenience, and objects that do not need to survive a postback all count against it. The transient keyword excludes a property from view state, which is why the same page passes in a lightly populated sandbox and fails against production data volumes.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (queries within governor limits) — a governor limit failure throws a limit exception, not a view state error.
Option C (properties marked private) — visibility has no effect on serialisation; private properties are still in view state.
Option D (profile access to the page) — a user without access gets an authorization error, not a view state one.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_visualforce_best_practices.meta/salesforce_visualforce_best_practices/pages_best_practices_perf_code_view_state.htm

question:
A company processes Orders within their Salesforce instance. When an Order's status changes to 'Paid' it must notify the company's order management system
(OMS). The OMS exposes SOAP web service endpoints to listen for when to retrieve the data from Salesforce.
What is the optimal method to implement this?
optionA: Generate the Enterprise WSDL and use it to make a callout to the OMS.
optionB: Generate the Partner WSDL and use it to make a callout to the OMS.
optionC: Create an Outbound Message that contains the session ID and send it to the OMS.
optionD: Create an Apex trigger and make a callout to the OMS from the trigger.
explanation:
Creating an Outbound Message and sending it to the OMS is the optimal method. It is declarative, it fires from a flow, workflow rule or approval process when the Order's status changes to Paid, it delivers a SOAP message to an endpoint of the kind the OMS already exposes, and it retries on its own: messages queue until they are delivered or until they are 24 hours old, with a 60-second timeout per attempt.
One detail in this item is now out of date. Outbound messages no longer carry a session id. Effective the week of 23 February 2026, Salesforce removed the Send Session ID option, forced IncludeSessionId to false, and stopped including the sessionID element in the payload; a system that calls back into Salesforce after receiving the notification must authenticate with OAuth 2.0. Choose the outbound message for the declarative, retrying SOAP delivery, not for a session id it no longer sends.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Enterprise WSDL callout) — backwards: the Enterprise WSDL describes Salesforce's own API for clients calling in, not the OMS's endpoint.
Option B (Partner WSDL callout) — the same mistake with the loosely typed WSDL.
Option D (callout from an Apex trigger) — works, but must be made asynchronously, consumes the transaction's callout budget, and makes you hand-build the retry behaviour outbound messaging already provides.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.workflow_om_considerations.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.workflow_managing_outbound_messages.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=005232763&language=en_US&type=1

corrected.note: Key C stands — outbound messaging is still the correct mechanism — but the stated rationale is no longer true. Salesforce removed the outbound-message session id in February 2026, so 'contains the session ID' describes a retired capability and must not be taught as a reason to pick this answer.

optionA: Line 1: class must be global
optionB: Lines 1 and 6: class and method must be global
optionC: Line 6: method must be static
optionD: Line 8: method must first serialize the list to JSON before returning
explanation:
The method must be static is what is wrong. An Apex method an Aura component calls from its client-side controller has to be annotated @AuraEnabled and declared static; a non-static @AuraEnabled method is exposed only as a property getter for a returned object, not as a callable server action, so the component's call fails.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (class must be global) — public is sufficient for a controller in the same namespace; global is only required for managed-package access across namespaces.
Option B (class and method must be global) — the same, for both.
Option D (serialize the list to JSON first) — the framework serialises the return value automatically; returning a List<String> is exactly what is expected.
References:

question:
An Apex class does not achieve expected code coverage. The testSetup method explicitly calls a method in the Apex class.
How can the developer generate the code coverage?
optionA: Verify the user has permissions passing a user into System.runAs().
optionB: Call the Apex class method from a testMethod instead of the testSetup method.
optionC: Add @testVisible to the method in the class the developer is testing.
optionD: Use system.assert() in testSetup to verify the values are being returned.
explanation:
Calling the Apex class method from a test method instead of the testSetup method is how the coverage is generated. Code executed only from an @testSetup method does not count toward coverage — coverage is measured from the paths test methods themselves exercise — so a class whose only invocation is in setup shows as uncovered no matter how much of it ran.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (pass a user into System.runAs()) — changes whose permissions apply, not which code counts as covered.
Option C (@TestVisible on the method) — only exposes private members to tests; it does not make setup-time execution count.
Option D (System.assert() in testSetup) — an assertion changes nothing about coverage, and setup code still does not count.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_testing_testsetup_using.htm

question:
A developer is trying to decide between creating a Visualforce component or a Lightning component for a custom screen.
Which functionality consideration impacts the final decision?
optionA: Does the screen need to be rendered as a PDF?
optionB: Does the screen need to be accessible from the Lightning Experience UI?
optionC: Will the screen make use of a JavaScript framework?
optionD: Will the screen be accessed via a mobile app?
explanation:
Whether the screen needs to be rendered as a PDF is the consideration that decides it. Visualforce supports renderAs="pdf" to output a page as a PDF; Lightning components have no native equivalent, so a PDF requirement forces the choice toward Visualforce.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (accessible from Lightning Experience) — both Visualforce pages and Lightning components run in Lightning Experience.
Option C (uses a JavaScript framework) — Visualforce can embed a framework and Lightning components are JavaScript by nature; neither is ruled out.
Option D (accessed via a mobile app) — both technologies can surface in the Salesforce mobile app.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.pages.meta/pages/pages_output_pdf_renderas.htm

question:
A developer wishes to improve runtime performance of Apex calls by caching results on the client.
What is the best way to implement this?
optionA: Decorate the server-side method with @AuraEnabled(cacheable=true).
optionB: Set a cookie in the browser for use upon return to the page.
optionC: Call the setStorable() method on the action in the JavaScript client-side code.
optionD: Decorate the server-side method with @AuraEnabled(storable=true).
explanation:
Decorating the server-side method with @AuraEnabled(cacheable=true) is the best way. It marks the method's results as cacheable on the client, so repeated calls with the same arguments are served from the framework's cache rather than a round trip to the server, and it is the single setting that works for both LWC and Aura.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (set a cookie) — a hand-rolled cache outside the framework's data layer, with none of its invalidation or refresh behaviour.
Option C (setStorable() on the action) — the older Aura-only mechanism; it is not available to Lightning web components and the server-side annotation is the recommended route.
Option D (@AuraEnabled(storable=true)) — no such attribute exists.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_classes_annotation_AuraEnabled.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.lightning.meta/lightning/controllers_server_storable_actions.htm

question:
A developer is asked to update data in an org based on new business rules. The new rules state that Accounts with the type set to 'Customer' should have a status of 'Active', and Accounts with the type set to 'Prospect' should have a status of 'Pending'. No other changes to data should be made.
Which code block will accurately meet the business requirements?
explanation:
The code block that scopes the query with WHERE Type IN :statusMap.keySet() and sets a.Status = statusMap.get(a.Type) is the one that meets the requirements. Both A and B write the correct Status values, so the field values are not what separates them — read the placement of accountUpdates.add(a) instead.
In B the query itself is scoped: it retrieves only Customers and Prospects, every record retrieved is one the rules apply to, and the new value comes straight out of the map, so the mapping is stated once.
In A the add() sits outside the containsKey guard, so every Account in the org lands in accountUpdates and the DML writes to all of them. The guard protects the field values but not the update. That matters in three concrete ways. Every one of those unrelated Accounts runs its update triggers, flows, and validation rules, so a single validation rule failing on a record that has nothing to do with this change fails the entire DML and nothing is updated at all. Their audit fields move even though no business field did. And the code does not survive volume: the unfiltered query is capped at 50,000 rows and the update at 10,000 records per transaction, so in an org large enough to care about this task, A throws before it finishes while B stays bounded by the number of Customers and Prospects.
The habit being tested is to scope the query to the records the requirement names, rather than querying everything and sorting it out in Apex.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (containsKey guard, add() outside it) — correct values, but every Account in the org is updated, which violates "no other changes to data should be made" and breaks on volume.
Option C (two isNotBlank checks, add() outside them) — the same defect as A in a more verbose form.
Option D (ternary with no guard) — wrong on values as well: it sets every Account whose Type is not 'Customer', including Accounts with no Type at all, to 'Pending'.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_gov_limits.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_triggers_bulk.htm

Both blocks assign the correct statuses, but in A the accountUpdates.add(a) call sits outside the containsKey guard, so the DML touches every Account in the org — which the stem's 'no other changes to data should be made' forbids, and which hits the 10,000-row DML and 50,000-row SOQL governor limits at scale. B filters the query by the map's keySet and updates only matching records. The previous explanation already conceded that 'B is actually the more optimized approach' and defended A only by appeal to a published exam key, which is not evidence.

question: What is a benefit of JavaScript remoting over Visualforce Remote Objects?
optionA: Allows for specified re-render targets
optionB: Does not require any Apex code
optionC: Does not require any JavaScript code
optionD: Supports complex server-side application logic
explanation:
Support for complex server-side application logic is the benefit. JavaScript remoting invokes @RemoteAction Apex methods, so it can run arbitrary business logic on the server and return custom results; Visualforce Remote Objects are a declarative proxy for basic CRUD and queries from JavaScript and cannot execute Apex at all.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (specified re-render targets) — that is the actionFunction/actionSupport model with reRender; neither remoting nor Remote Objects re-renders page regions.
Option B (does not require any Apex code) — backwards: it is Remote Objects that needs no Apex, while remoting exists to call Apex.
Option C (does not require any JavaScript code) — both are JavaScript-driven.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.pages.meta/pages/pages_js_remoting.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.pages.meta/pages/pages_remote_objects.htm

question:
A Lightning Component functions in preview mode and needs to be used inside a Lightning App Builder page, but it is not available.
What change should be applied to the component?
optionA: Expose it in the markup using the implements and access attributes.
optionB: Delete the component, metadata, and Apex controller and recreate them.
optionC: Refresh the sandbox and upgrade it to the latest API version.
optionD: Look for errors in the logic in the JavaScript controller.
explanation:
Exposing it in the markup using the implements and access attributes is the change. To appear in the Lightning App Builder a component must declare the appropriate interface through implements (for example flexipage:availableForAllPageTypes) and be exposed with access="global"; since the component already works in preview, its logic is fine and only that exposure is missing.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (delete and recreate everything) — recreating the same markup reproduces the same omission.
Option C (refresh the sandbox and upgrade the API version) — neither affects whether a component is exposed to App Builder.
Option D (look for errors in the JavaScript controller) — a component that functions in preview has working logic; the problem is availability, not behaviour.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.lightning.meta/lightning/components_config_for_app_builder.htm

question:
Recently a Salesforce org's integration failed because it exceeded the number of allowed API calls in a 24-hour period. The integration handles a near real-time, complex insertion of data into Salesforce.
The flow of data is as follows:
✑ The integration looks up Contact records with a given email address and, if found, the integration adds a Task to the first matching Contact it finds.
✑ If a match is not found, the integration looks up Lead records with a given email address and, if found, the integration adds a Task to the first matching Lead it finds.
✑ If a match is not found, the integration will create a Lead and a Task for that newly created Lead.
What is one way in which the integration can stay near real-time, but not exceed the number of allowed API calls in a 24-hour period?
optionA: Use the REST API as well as the SOAP API to effectively double the API calls allowed in a 24-hour period.
optionB: Create an Inbound Message that, using Flow, can do all of the logic the integration code was doing.
optionC: Write a custom Apex web service that, given an email address, does all of the logic the integration code was doing
optionD: Create several Apex InboundEmailHandlers to accept calls from the third-party system, thus bypassing the API limits.
explanation:
Writing a custom Apex web service that, given an email address, does all of the logic is the way. One call from the external system then performs the whole sequence server-side — find a Contact, else a Lead, else create a Lead and its Task — so what used to cost several API calls per record costs one, which keeps the integration near real-time while staying under the 24-hour limit.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (use REST and SOAP to double the allowance) — the API request limit is per org across all APIs; using two does not double it.
Option B (an Inbound Message with Flow) — there is no such feature; outbound messages exist, inbound ones do not.
Option D (several Apex InboundEmailHandlers) — email services are for processing inbound email, not API calls, and email delivery is not near real-time.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_rest.htm

question:
A company wants to build a custom Lightning Component that will display a specified Account Field Set and that can only be added to the Account record page.
Which design resource configuration should be used?
optionA:
<design:component label="Account FS Component">
    <design:attribute name="fieldSetName" Label="Field Set Name" />
    <sfdc:objects>
        <sfdc:object>FieldSet</sfdc:object>

optionB:

    <sfdc:objects>

question: A developer notices the execution of all the test methods in a class takes a long time to run, due to the initial setup of all the test data that is needed to perform the tests. What should the developer do to speed up test execution?
optionA: Define a method that creates test data and annotate with @testSetup.
optionB: Define a method that creates test data and annotate with @createData.
optionC: Ensure proper usage of test data factory in all test methods.
optionD: Reduce the amount of test methods in the class.
explanation:
Defining a method that creates the test data and annotating it with @testSetup is what speeds up the class. A @testSetup method runs once per test class and its records are provided to, and reset for, every test method, so the prerequisite data is created a single time instead of in each method.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (@createData annotation) — no such annotation exists.
Option C (a test data factory in every method) — a factory tidies the code but still runs per method unless it is called from @testSetup.
Option D (fewer test methods) — sacrifices coverage to save time.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_testing_testsetup_using.htm

question:
Which three Visualforce components can be used to initiate Ajax behavior to perform partial page updates?
Choose 3 answers.
optionA: <apex:commandLink>
optionB: <apex:commandButton>
optionC: <Apex:form>
optionD: <apex:actionsStatus>
explanation:
<apex:commandLink>, <apex:commandButton> and <apex:actionSupport> are the three. commandLink and commandButton submit the form to the server and, with reRender, refresh only the parts of the page named; actionSupport attaches AJAX behaviour to another component's browser event, such as onchange, and triggers a partial update from there.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option C (<apex:form>) — the container that makes a postback possible; it does not initiate anything on its own.
Option D (<apex:actionStatus>) — displays the status of an AJAX request that something else started.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.pages.meta/pages/pages_compref_actionSupport.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.pages.meta/pages/pages_compref_commandButton.htm

question:
A developer built an Aura component for guests to self-register upon arrival at a front desk kiosk. Now the developer needs to create a component for the utility tray to alert users whenever a guest arrives at the front desk.
What should be used?
optionA: DML Operation
optionB: Changelog
optionC: Application Event
optionD: Component Event
explanation:
An Application Event is what should be used. The self-registration component and the utility-tray component are not in the same containment hierarchy, and an Aura application event is broadcast to every component in the app that registers a handler for it, wherever it sits — so the tray can learn of the arrival without any parent-child relationship to the kiosk component.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (DML operation) — writes a record; it notifies no component.
Option B (Changelog) — not an Aura mechanism.
Option D (Component Event) — propagates up the containment hierarchy only, so a component in a separate tree never receives it.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.lightning.meta/lightning/events_application.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.lightning.meta/lightning/events_component.htm

question:
A company has a custom object, Order__c, that has a custom picklist field, Status__c, with values of `"New',
`"In Progress', or `"Fulfilled' and a lookup field,
Contact__c, to Contact.
Which SOQL query will return a unique list of all the Contact records that have no `"Fulfilled' Orders?
optionA:
SELECT Id FROM Contact WHERE Id NOT IN (SELECT Id FROM Order__c WHERE Status__c =
'Fulfilled')
optionB: SELECT Contact__c FROM Order__c WHERE Status__c <> 'Fulfilled'
optionC: SELECT Id FROM Contact WHERE Id NOT IN (SELECT Contact__c FROM Order__c WHERE Status__c = 'Fulfilled')
optionD: SELECT Contact__c FROM Order__c WHERE Id NOT IN (SELECT Id FROM Order__c Where Status__c = 'Fulfilled')
explanation:
SELECT Id FROM Contact WHERE Id NOT IN (SELECT Contact__c FROM Order__c WHERE Status__c = 'Fulfilled') is the query. Selecting from Contact gives each Contact once, and the semi-join subquery returns the Contact__c of every fulfilled Order, so NOT IN excludes exactly the Contacts that have at least one fulfilled Order.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (NOT IN (SELECT Id FROM Order__c ...)) — compares Contact Ids against Order Ids, which never match, so every Contact is returned.
Option B (SELECT Contact__c FROM Order__c WHERE Status__c <> 'Fulfilled') — returns one row per non-fulfilled Order, with duplicates, and still includes Contacts that also have a fulfilled Order.
Option D (SELECT Contact__c FROM Order__c WHERE Id NOT IN ...) — the same shape as B: rows are Orders, not unique Contacts, and a Contact with both kinds of Order still appears.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.soql_sosl.meta/soql_sosl/sforce_api_calls_soql_relationships_query_using.htm

question:
A developer is writing a Visualforce page that queries accounts in the system and presents a data table with the results. The users want to be able to filter the results based on up to five fields. However, the users want to pick the five fields to use as filter fields when they run the page.
Which Apex code feature is required to facilitate this solution?
optionA: Streaming API
optionB: Metadata API
optionC: variable binding
optionD: dynamic SOQL
explanation:
Dynamic SOQL is the required feature. The filter fields are chosen at run time, so the query cannot be written in advance; building the SOQL string from the user's selections and executing it with Database.query() is what lets the page filter on whichever five fields the user picks.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Streaming API) — delivers real-time event notifications; it does not query records for a page.
Option B (Metadata API) — manages the org's metadata, not its data.
Option C (variable binding) — binds values into a query you have already written; it cannot change which fields the WHERE clause names.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_dynamic_soql.htm

question:
Universal Containers is leading a development team that follows the source-driven development approach in Salesforce. As part of their continuous integration and delivery (CL/CD) process, they need to automatically deploy changes to multiple environments, including sandbox and production.
'Which mechanism or tool would best support their CI/CD pipeline in source-driven development?
optionA: Salesforce CLI with Salesforce DX
optionB: Salesforce Extensions for Visual Studio Code
optionC: Change Sets
optionD: Ant Migration Tool
explanation:
Salesforce CLI with Salesforce DX is the mechanism. It is built for source-driven development — the source of truth lives in version control, and the CLI's commands to create scratch orgs, run tests and deploy source can be scripted by any CI server, so the same pipeline can push to sandboxes and production automatically.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Salesforce Extensions for Visual Studio Code) — an IDE integration a developer drives by hand; it is not what a pipeline runs.
Option C (Change Sets) — org-to-org, point-and-click and manual, with no source control and nothing to automate.
Option D (Ant Migration Tool) — scriptable, but it works on Metadata API retrieve-and-deploy packages rather than a source-driven project, and it is the approach DX replaced.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_ci.htm

question:
A developer is tasked with ensuring that email addresses entered into the system for Contacts and for a custom object called survey Response c do not belong to a list of blocked domains.
The list of blocked domains is stored in a custom object for ease of maintenance by users. The survey Response c object is populated via a custom Visualforce page.
What is the optimal way to implement this?
optionA: Implement the logic in validation rules on the Contact and the Burvey Response_c Objects.
optionB: Implement the logic in a helper class that is called by an Apex trigger on Contact and from the custom Visualforce page controller.
optionC: Implement the logic in an Apex trigger on Contact and also implement the logic within the custom Visualforce page controller.
optionD: Implement the logic in the custom Visualforce page controller and call "that method from an Apex trigger on Contact.
explanation:
Implementing the logic in a helper class that is called by an Apex trigger on Contact and from the custom Visualforce page controller is the optimal implementation. The blocked-domain check has to run in two places, and putting it in one class that both call keeps a single copy of the logic, a single query of the blocked-domains object, and a single place to test and change.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (validation rules on both objects) — a validation rule formula cannot query the records of an unrelated custom object, so it cannot read the maintained list of blocked domains.
Option C (duplicate the logic in the trigger and in the controller) — two copies that will drift apart.
Option D (logic in the page controller, called from the trigger) — makes a data-layer trigger depend on a UI controller; the dependency runs the wrong way.

https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.fields_validation_rules_fields.htm&language=en_US&type=5
