question:
A company notices that their unit tests in a test class with many methods to create many records for prerequisite reference data are slow.
What can a developer to do address the issue?
optionA: Turn off triggers, flows, and validations when running tests.
optionB: Move the prerequisite reference data setup to a TestDataFactory and call that from each test method.
optionC: Move the prerequisite reference data setup to a @testSetup method in the test class.
optionD: Move the prerequisite reference data setup to the constructor for the test class.
explanation:
Moving the prerequisite reference data setup to a @testSetup method in the test class is what addresses the issue. The method runs once per class and every test method then starts from that data, rolled back between methods, so the reference records are created once rather than once per test.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (turn off triggers, flows and validations) — there is no switch for that in a test run, and disabling them would make the tests exercise behaviour the org does not have.
Option B (a TestDataFactory called from each method) — tidier code, but the records are still created once per method, so the time is unchanged.
Option D (the test class constructor) — Apex test classes do not use a constructor for setup; the platform runs @testSetup and test methods directly.

question:
<!-- Lightning Web Component HTML file -->

<template>
    <lightning-button label="Call server" onclick={handleClick}></lightning-button>
</template>

// Lightning Web Component JS file

import {LightningElement} from 'lwc';
import serverEcho from '@salesforce/apex/SimpleServerSideController.serverEcho';

export default class HelloWorld extends LightningElement {
    firstName = 'World';
    
    handleClick() {
        serverEcho({ firstName: this.firstName })
            .then((result) => {
                alert('From Server: ' + result);
            })
            .catch((error) => {
                console.error(error);
            });
    }
}

// Apex Controller for Lightning Component

public with sharing class SimpleServerSideController {
    @AuraEnabled
    public static String serverEcho(Object firstName) {
        String firstNameStr = (String)firstName.get('firstName');
        return ('Hello from the server, ' + firstNameStr);
    }
}
Given the code above, which two changes need to be made in the Apex Controller for the code to work?
optionA: Annotate the entire class as @AuraEnabled instead of just the single method.
optionB: Change the argument in the Apex Controller line 05 from subject to string.
optionC: Change the method signature to be global static, not public to String.
optionD: Remove line 06 from the Apex Controller and instead use firstName in the return on line 07.
explanation:
Changing the argument on line 05 from Object to String, and removing line 06 to use firstName directly in the return, are the two changes. The component calls serverEcho({ firstName: this.firstName }), and an imperative Apex call passes an object whose property names match the Apex method's parameter names. So the Apex parameter has to be named firstName and typed to what the component actually sends — a String. Declaring it as Object is what breaks the call.
Once the parameter is a String, line 06 has nothing left to do: firstName already holds the value, and .get('firstName') is a Map operation that a String does not have. Remove that line and return firstName directly.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (annotate the entire class as @AuraEnabled) — the annotation goes on the method, not on the class; annotating the class does not expose anything.
Option C (change the signature to global static) — an @AuraEnabled method already has to be static and public or global, so switching to global changes nothing about the argument that is actually failing.

https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/lwc/guide/apex-call-imperative.html

question:
A developer is writing a Jest test for a Lightning web component that conditionally displays child components based on a user's checkbox selections.
What should the developer do to properly test that the correct components display and hide for each scenario?
optionA: Create a new describe block for each test.
optionB: Reset the DOM after each test with the after Each() method.
optionC: Add a teardown block to reset the DOM after each test.
optionD: Create a new jsdom instance for each test.
explanation:
Resetting the DOM after each test with the afterEach() method is what the developer should do. Jest shares one jsdom document across the test cases in a file, so the components one test renders are still in the document when the next one runs; clearing document.body in afterEach() is the standard Jest teardown and gives each scenario a clean DOM.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a new describe block per test) — describe groups tests; it does not reset the DOM between them.
Option C (a teardown block) — Jest has no "teardown" block; its teardown hooks are afterEach() and afterAll().
Option D (a new jsdom instance per test) — the jsdom environment is created once per test file by Jest; you do not instantiate it per test.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/lwc/guide/unit-testing-using-jest-create-tests.html

question:
A developer has a Visualforce page that automatically assigns ownership of an Account to a queue upon save.
The page appears to correctly assign ownership, but an assertion validating the correct ownership fails.
What can cause this problem?
optionA: The test class does not retrieve the updated value from the database.
optionB: The test class does not use the Bulk API for loading test data.
optionC: The test class does not use the SeeAllData=true annotation.
optionD: The test class does not implement the Queueable interface.
explanation:
The test class not retrieving the updated value from the database is the cause. The page's save logic changes the owner on the record in the database, but the Account variable the test still holds is the in-memory copy from before the save; asserting on it sees the old OwnerId. The test has to re-query the Account after the operation and assert on the fresh row.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Bulk API for test data) — the Bulk API is for loading large volumes from outside the org; it has nothing to do with a unit test's assertions.
Option C (SeeAllData=true) — widens what the test can query; the record here was created by the test and is already visible.
Option D (implement Queueable) — a test class does not implement Queueable, and nothing in this scenario is asynchronous.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_testing_best_practices.htm

question:
A developer needs to store variables to control the style and behavior of a Lightning Web Component.
Which feature can be used to ensure that the variables are testable in both Production and all Sandboxes?
optionA: Custom setting
optionB: Custom object
optionC: Custom variable
optionD: Custom metadata
explanation:
Custom metadata is the feature. Custom metadata type records are metadata, so they deploy with the component through change sets, packages or source deployment and are visible to tests in every environment without SeeAllData; the same configuration therefore exists, and is testable, in production and in every sandbox.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (custom setting) — its values are data, not metadata: they do not deploy, and a test cannot see them without SeeAllData=true or inserting them itself.
Option B (custom object) — records are data too, with the same deployment and test-visibility problems.
Option C (custom variable) — not a Salesforce feature.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.custommetadatatypes_overview.htm&language=en_US&type=5

optionA: Instances of Apex classes, such as MyDataWrapper, cannot be returned to a Lightning component.
optionB: The member's Name and option should not have getter and setter.
optionC: The member's Name and option should not be declared public.
optionD: The member's Name and option of the class MyDataWrapper should be annotated with @AuraEnabled also.
explanation:
The members Name and option of MyDataWrapper should be annotated with @AuraEnabled as well. The framework serialises only the properties of a returned Apex object that carry the annotation; without it MyDataWrapper comes back to the Aura component with no data in it, which is exactly what "not getting anything back" looks like.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (instances of Apex classes cannot be returned) — they can, provided their members are @AuraEnabled.
Option B (Name and option should not have getters and setters) — properties with get; set; are the normal shape for an @AuraEnabled member.
Option C (Name and option should not be public) — they must be public to be exposed; making them private would hide them.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_classes_annotation_AuraEnabled.htm

question:
Universal Containers needs to integrate with their own, existing, internal custom web application. The web application accepts JSON payloads, resizes product images, and sends the resized images back to Salesforce.
What should the developer use to implement this integration?
optionA: An Apex trigger that calls an @future method that allows callouts
optionB: A platform event that makes a callout to the web application
optionC: A flow that calls an @future method that allows callouts
optionD: A flow with an outbound message that contains a session ID
explanation:
An Apex trigger that calls an @future method that allows callouts is what the developer should use. The integration needs a JSON payload sent to the web application and its response handled, which is Apex callout work, and a callout cannot be made synchronously from a trigger — so the trigger hands the record ids to an @future(callout=true) method that runs after the transaction commits and makes the HTTP request.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (a platform event that makes a callout) — an event does not make callouts; something would still have to subscribe to it and call out asynchronously.
Option C (a flow that calls an @future method) — a flow calls @InvocableMethod methods, and an invocable method cannot itself be @future.
Option D (a flow with an outbound message containing a session ID) — outbound messages send SOAP, not JSON, cannot receive the resized images, and no longer carry a session id at all.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_classes_annotation_future.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_callouts_timeouts.htm

question: Which statement is considered a best practice for writing bulk safe Apex triggers?
optionA: Add records to collections and perform DML operations against these collections.
optionB: Add LIMIT 50000 to every SOQL statement.
optionC: Perform all DML operations from within a future method.
optionD: Use the Database methods with allorNone set to £21s= instead of DML statements.
explanation:
Adding records to collections and performing DML operations against those collections is the best practice. A trigger receives up to 200 records at a time, so DML inside a loop consumes one of the 150 DML statements per record; collecting the records to change and issuing a single insert or update outside the loop keeps the trigger within limits at any batch size.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (LIMIT 50000 on every SOQL statement) — a limit clause does nothing about how many queries run; the bulk-safety problem is queries in loops, not row counts.
Option C (all DML from a future method) — moves the work out of the transaction, adds asynchronous complexity, and is still subject to the same per-transaction limits inside the future call.
Option D (Database methods with allOrNone false) — partial-success DML is about error handling, not about how many DML statements a bulk trigger issues.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_triggers_bulk.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_triggers_bulk_idioms.htm

question: Universal Containers is using a custom Salesforce application to manage customer support cases. The support team needs to collaborate with external partners to resolve certain cases. However, they want to control the visibility and access to the cases shared with the external partners. Which Salesforce feature can help achieve this requirement?
optionA: Role hierarchy
optionB: Criteria-based sharing rules
optionC: Apex managed sharing
optionD: Sharing sets
explanation:
Sharing sets are the feature built for exactly this shape of problem. Salesforce Help describes a sharing set as granting Experience Cloud site users access to any record associated with an account or contact that matches the user's own account or contact, configured through access mappings that follow lookups from the user and from the target record. The article's own example is the scenario in this question: grant site users access to all cases related to the account identified on the user's contact.
That is what makes it the controlled option. Access is scoped by the partner's own account rather than granted wholesale, it is declarative, and record access granted this way is deliberately not extended upward through the role hierarchy.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (role hierarchy) — models the internal organisation; it does not describe which cases an external partner may see.
Option B (criteria-based sharing rules) — key off field values on the record rather than off the relationship between the record and the external user's account, so they can't express "the cases belonging to this partner's account".
Option C (Apex managed sharing) — could be made to do it, but the platform sharing guidance is to reach for code only when a requirement can't be met by any other means, and here it can.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.networks_setting_light_users.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://architect.salesforce.com/fundamentals/platform-sharing-architecture

question: Which method should be used to convert a Date to a String in the current user's locale?
optionA: String.format
optionB: Date.paras
optionC: Date. format
optionD: String.valueof
explanation:
Date.format() is the method. It converts a Date to a String using the running user's locale, so the same call yields 31/12/2026 for one user and 12/31/2026 for another, with no formatting code of your own.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (String.format) — a general substitution method; it does not know how a date should look in a locale.
Option B (Date.parse) — the reverse direction: it turns a locale-formatted String into a Date.
Option D (String.valueOf) — converts a Date to a String in a fixed yyyy-MM-dd form, ignoring the user's locale.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexref.meta/apexref/apex_methods_system_date.htm

question:
Universal Containers uses Big Objects to store almost a billion customer transactions called Customer_Transaction__b.
These are the fields on Customer_Transaction__b:
Account__c -
Program__c -
Points_Earned__c -
Location__c -
Transaction_Date__c -
The following fields have been identified as Index Fields for the Customer_Transaction__b object:
Account__c, Program__c, and Transaction_Date__c.
Which SOQL query is valid on the Customer_Transaction__b Big Object?
optionA: SELECT Account__c, Program__c, Transaction_Date__c FROM Customer_Transaction__b WHERE Account__c = '001R000000302D3' AND Program__c ='Shoppers' AND Transaction_Date__c=2019-05-31T00:00Z
optionB: SELECT Account__c, Program__c, Transaction_Date__c FROM Customer_Transaction__b WHERE Account__c = '001R000000302D3' AND Program__c LIKE 'Shop%' AND Transaction_Date__c=2019-05-31T00:00Z
optionC: SELECT Account__c, Program__c, Transaction_Date__c FROM Customer_Transaction__b WHERE Account__c = '001R000000302D3' AND Program__c INCLUDES ('Shoppers', 'Womens') AND Transaction_Date__c=2019-05-31T00:00Z
optionD: SELECT Account__c, Program__c, Transaction_Date__c FROM Customer_Transaction__b WHERE Account__c = '001R000000302D3' AND Program__c EXCLUDES ('Shoppers', 'Womens') AND Transaction_Date__c=2019-05-31T00:00Z
explanation:
The query filtering all three index fields with equality — Account__c, Program__c and Transaction_Date__c — is the valid one. A big object query must filter the index fields in the order they were defined, using only the operators the index supports: =, <, >, <=, >= and IN.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Program__c LIKE 'Shop%') — LIKE is not a supported operator on a big object index field.
Option C (Program__c INCLUDES (...)) — INCLUDES is a multi-select picklist operator and is not supported here.
Option D (Program__c EXCLUDES (...)) — EXCLUDES is the same: unsupported, so the query fails at runtime.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/2026/06/big-objects-playbook-payload-capture-and-replay
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.bigobjects.meta/bigobjects/big_object_query_examples.htm

optionA: Implement SeeAllData=true to ensure the Queueable job is able to run in bulk mode.
optionB: Ensure the running user of the test class has at least the View All permission on the Order object.
optionC: Enclose System.enqueueJob(new OrderQueueableJob()) within Test.startTest() and Test.stopTest().
optionD: Implement Test.isRunningTest() to prevent chaining jobs during test execution.
explanation:
Enclosing System.enqueueJob(new OrderQueueableJob()) within Test.startTest() and Test.stopTest(), and implementing Test.isRunningTest() to prevent chaining during the test, are the two actions. A queueable is asynchronous, and the platform runs everything queued inside that block synchronously once Test.stopTest() is reached, so assertions placed afterwards actually see the job's results. And OrderQueueableJob calls System.enqueueJob again from inside execute(): chaining a further job during a test run raises an error, so the standard pattern is to wrap that inner enqueue in a Test.isRunningTest() check and let the chain stop at the first link under test.
Worth knowing: the chaining-in-a-test restriction is long-standing platform behaviour but is no longer stated on the Queueable Apex page. What that page does document is that only one job can be enqueued from an executing job, and the startTest/stopTest pattern this answer relies on.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (SeeAllData=true for "bulk mode") — widens data access and has no bearing on asynchronous execution; there is no bulk mode for a queueable to run in.
Option B (View All on Order for the running user) — changes what the user can see, which is not why the test fails.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_queueing_jobs.htm

question: Which use case can only be performed by using asynchronous apex?
optionA: Scheduling a batch process to complete in the future
optionB: Processing high volumes of records
optionC: Updating a record after the completion of an insert
optionD: Calling a web service from an Apex trigger
explanation:
Calling a web service from an Apex trigger is the use case only asynchronous Apex can perform. A trigger runs synchronously, and Salesforce does not permit a synchronous callout from trigger context — attempting one raises "Callout from triggers are currently not supported". The only way to call a web service from a trigger is to hand the work to asynchronous Apex: an @future(callout=true) method or a Queueable. That makes this a use case where synchronous Apex is not merely slower but forbidden.
Option A is the weak distractor here and worth naming: scheduling a batch to run later does require the Schedulable interface, which is itself asynchronous Apex, so read literally it is also something "only performed by asynchronous Apex". The discriminator the item is reaching for is the callout, where a synchronous attempt is actively rejected by the platform rather than merely unavailable.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (scheduling a batch process) — asynchronous by nature, but the exam's intended discriminator is the case the platform rejects outright, and that is the callout.
Option B (processing high volumes of records) — done synchronously every day; volume pushes you toward Batch Apex for governor headroom, not because a synchronous approach is impossible.
Option C (updating a record after an insert) — an after insert trigger or a second DML statement does this synchronously.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_callouts_timeouts.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_classes_annotation_future.htm

question:
Given the following containment hierarchy:
What is the correct way to communicate the new value of a property named "passthrough" to my-parent-component if the property is defined within my-child-component?
optionA:
let cEvent = new CustomEvent('passthrough', { detail: 'this.passthrough' });
this.dispatchEvent(cEvent);
optionB:
let cEvent = new CustomEvent('passthrough');
this.dispatchEvent(cEvent);
optionC:
let cEvent = new CustomEvent('passthrough', { detail: this.passthrough });
this.dispatchEvent(cEvent);
optionD:
let cEvent = new CustomEvent(@passthrough);
this.dispatchEvent(cEvent);
explanation:
new CustomEvent('passthrough', { detail: this.passthrough }) followed by this.dispatchEvent(cEvent) is the correct way. The child creates a CustomEvent named passthrough, puts the property's actual value in the detail payload, and dispatches it; the parent listens with onpassthrough and reads event.detail.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (detail: 'this.passthrough') — passes the string literal 'this.passthrough' rather than the property's value.
Option B (no detail) — the event fires, but carries no value for the parent to read.
Option D (new CustomEvent(@passthrough)) — not valid JavaScript.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/lwc/guide/events-create-dispatch.html

question:
A developer is inserting, updating, and deleting multiple lists of records in a single transaction and wants to ensure that any error prevents all execution.
How should the developer implement error exception handling in their code to handle this?
optionA: Use Database methods to obtain lists of Database.SaveResults.
optionB: Use a try-catch statement and handle DML cleanup in the catch statement.
optionC: Use Database.setSavepoint() and Database.rollBack with a try-catch statement.
optionD: Use a try-catch and use sObject.addError() on any failures.
explanation:
Database.setSavepoint() and Database.rollback() with a try-catch statement is how to implement it. Set the savepoint before the first DML, wrap the inserts, updates and deletes in the try block, and roll back to the savepoint in the catch — so a failure anywhere in the sequence undoes every earlier statement and nothing partial is committed.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Database methods returning SaveResults) — partial-success mode is the opposite of what is wanted: it lets the successful records commit while reporting the failures.
Option B (try-catch with DML cleanup in the catch) — hand-written compensating DML is fragile and may itself fail; a rollback is the mechanism built for this.
Option D (try-catch with sObject.addError()) — addError() is for rejecting records inside a trigger; it does not undo DML already performed.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/langCon_apex_transaction_control.htm

question:
When the sales team views an individual customer record, they need to see recent interactions for the customer. These interactions can be sales orders, phone calls, or Cases. The date range for recent interactions will be different for every customer record type.
How can this be accomplished?
optionA: Use batch Apex to query for the most recent interactions when the customer view screen is loaded.
optionB: Use Lightning Flow to read the customer's record type, and then do a dynamic query for recent interactions and display on the View page.
optionC: Use a Lightning component to query and display interactions based on record type that is passed in using a design:attribute from the Lightning page.
optionD: Use a dynamic form on the customer record page to display recent interactions.
explanation:
A Lightning component that queries and displays interactions based on a record type passed in through a design:attribute from the Lightning page is how this can be accomplished. The component sits on the record page, the admin sets the record-type-specific configuration per page in App Builder, and the component's Apex queries sales orders, calls and Cases for the right date range and renders them with full control over the UI.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (batch Apex when the screen loads) — batch Apex is background processing for large volumes; it cannot return results to a page as it loads.
Option B (a Flow reading the record type and querying) — could be made to work on a record page, but a flow screen is a weak vehicle for a data-rich related list and offers far less control than a component.
Option D (a dynamic form) — dynamic forms lay out the record's own fields; they do not query or display related records.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.lightning.meta/lightning/components_config_for_app_builder_design_files.htm

question:
A developer is responsible for formulating the deployment process for a Salesforce project. The project follows a source-driven development approach, and the developer wants to ensure efficient deployment and version control of the metadata changes.
Which tool or mechanism should be utilized for managing the source-driven deployment process?
optionA: Metadata API
optionB: Change Sets
optionC: Force.com IDE
optionD: Salesforce CLI with Salesforce DX
explanation:
Salesforce CLI with Salesforce DX is the tool. It is designed around source-driven development: metadata lives as source in version control, and the CLI deploys, retrieves, tests and creates scratch orgs from the command line, so the whole process is scriptable and repeatable.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Metadata API) — the underlying transport the tools use; on its own it is not a deployment process or a version-control workflow.
Option B (Change Sets) — org-to-org, manual and without source control.
Option C (Force.com IDE) — a retired Eclipse plug-in; it is no longer supported.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_ci.htm

optionA: Create AccountHistory records manually in the test setup and write a query to get them.
optionB: Use @isTest(SeeAllData=true) to see historical data from the org and query for AccountHistory records.
optionC: Use Test.isRunningTest() in getAccountHistory() to conditionally return fake AccountHistory records.
optionD: The test method should be deleted since this code cannot be tested.
explanation:
Using Test.isRunningTest() in getAccountHistory() to conditionally return fake AccountHistory records is what should be done. AccountHistory is a system-maintained, read-only object: Salesforce writes a row when a tracked field on the parent Account changes, and no DML of yours can insert one, so a test cannot produce the rows the method depends on. Gating getAccountHistory() on Test.isRunningTest() and returning constructed AccountHistory rows lets the method be exercised without depending on data the platform will not produce in a test. Be clear that this is a workaround, not a pattern to reach for: production code branching on whether it is under test is a well-known smell, and the durable fix is to put the query behind a seam — a selector class or an injected dependency — that the test can substitute.
One caveat about this item as printed: the test method shown queries AccountHistory directly rather than calling getAccountHistory(), so a stub inside that method would not actually change this test's result. Treat the answer as being about how to test code that depends on field history, not about this exact snippet.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (create AccountHistory records manually) — AccountHistory is read-only; the insert is not allowed.
Option B (SeeAllData=true) — only widens what the test can see in existing org data; the assertion is scoped to the Account the test just created, which has no history rows, so it fails just the same.
Option D (delete the test) — abandons coverage of a method that does have testable logic.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?language=en_US&id=sf.tracking_field_history.htm&type=5

https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_testing_data_access.htm

question:
A developer writes a Lightning web component that displays a dropdown list of all custom objects in the org from which a user will select. An Apex method prepares and returns data to the component.
What should the developer do to determine which objects to include in the response?
optionA: Check the isCustom() value on the sObject describe result.
optionB: Import the list of all custom objects from @salesforce/schema.
optionC: Check the getObjectType() value for 'Custom' or 'Standard' on the sObject describe result.
optionD: Use the getCustomObjects() method from the Schema class.
explanation:
Checking the isCustom() value on the sObject describe result is how to decide. Schema.getGlobalDescribe() returns every sObject type in the org; calling getDescribe() on each gives a DescribeSObjectResult whose isCustom() returns true for custom objects, so the Apex method can filter the list to those before returning it.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (import the list from @salesforce/schema) — the schema module imports references to specific objects and fields you name; it cannot enumerate the org's objects.
Option C (getObjectType() returning 'Custom' or 'Standard') — no such describe method; the describe result's type methods return tokens, not those strings.
Option D (Schema.getCustomObjects()) — does not exist.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexref.meta/apexref/apex_methods_system_sobject_describe.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_dynamic_describeSObject.htm

optionA: Use the cacheable=true attribute in the Apex method.
optionB: Ensure the OWD for the Opportunity object is Public.
optionC: Edit the code to use the without sharing keyword in the Apex class.
optionD: Use the Continuation=true attribute in the Apex method.
explanation:
Using the cacheable=true attribute in the Apex method is the modification. A method wired with @wire must be annotated @AuraEnabled(cacheable=true); findMyOpportunities is @AuraEnabled only, so the wire service rejects it and the component reports the error. Marking the method cacheable is also correct for what it does — a read-only query with no DML.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (make the Opportunity OWD Public) — the query is for the user's own Opportunities, which the owner can always see; sharing is not the problem.
Option C (without sharing) — the same: the owner already sees their own records, and the error is about the wire contract, not access.
Option D (Continuation=true) — not an @AuraEnabled attribute; Continuations are a mechanism for long-running callouts.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/lwc/guide/apex-wire-method.html
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/lwc/guide/data-wire-service-about.html

Users of this Visualforce page complain that the page does a full refresh every time the Search button is pressed.

optionA: Enclose the DATA table within the <apex:actionRegion> tag.
optionB: Implement the render attribute on the <apex:commandButton> tag.

optionD: implement the <apex:actionfunction> tag with immediate = true
explanation:
Implementing the reRender attribute on the <apex:commandButton> tag is what the developer should do (the option prints it as "render"). reRender names the ids of the components to redraw when the action completes; setting it to opportunityList makes the button's postback an AJAX request that repaints only that pageBlockSection instead of the whole page.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (enclose the data table in <apex:actionRegion>) — actionRegion limits which part of the form is submitted, not which part is redrawn.
Option C (make the search method return null) — returning null keeps the user on the same page but the page still reloads in full.
Option D (<apex:actionFunction> with immediate="true") — immediate skips validation and the apply-request-values phase; it has nothing to do with partial rendering.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.pages.meta/pages/pages_compref_commandButton.htm

question:
A developer wrote an Apex class to make several callouts to an external system.
If the URLs used in these callouts will change often, which feature should the developer use to minimize changes needed to the Apex class?
optionA: Session Id
optionB: Connected Apps
optionC: Named Credentials
optionD: Remote Site Settings
explanation:
Named Credentials are the feature. A named credential holds the endpoint URL and the authentication in Setup; the Apex refers to it as callout:Name and Salesforce substitutes the URL at runtime, so when the URL changes an administrator edits the named credential and the class is untouched.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Session Id) — an authentication token for calls into Salesforce; it has nothing to do with where an outbound callout goes.
Option B (Connected Apps) — let external applications authenticate into Salesforce; they do not hold outbound endpoints.
Option D (Remote Site Settings) — merely allow-list a domain for callouts; the URL itself still lives in the Apex.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?language=en_US&id=sf.named_credentials_about.htm&type=5

question:
A developer has a test class that creates test data before making a mock callout but now receives a 'You have uncommitted work pending. Please commit or rollback before calling out' error.
Which step should be taken to resolve the error?
optionA: Ensure both the Insertion and mock callout occur after the Test.stopTest().
optionB: Ensure the records are inserted before the Test.startTest() statement and the mock callout occurs within a method annotated with @testSetup.
optionC: Ensure both the insertion and mock callout occur after the Test.startTest().
optionD: Ensure the records are inserted before the Test.startTest() statement and the mock callout occurs after the Test.startTest().
explanation:
Inserting the records before the Test.startTest() statement and making the mock callout after it is the step. The Apex Developer Guide states the rule and its workaround in one place: callouts aren't allowed after DML operations in the same transaction, because the DML leaves pending uncommitted work. To insert test data and still make a mock callout, enclose the callout in Test.startTest and Test.stopTest and keep the DML outside that block — so the inserts run before Test.startTest and the callout runs after it. The same page adds that Test.startTest must appear before Test.setMock.
Two things are worth stating precisely. Test.startTest does not commit the inserted records; nothing in a test is ever committed. It opens a fresh context with its own set of governor limits, and it is that boundary the callout restriction is evaluated against. And the rule is not that every callout must precede every DML statement — DML that happens after a mock callout is explicitly allowed and needs no special handling.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (both after Test.stopTest()) — the insert and the callout share one context again, so the same error fires.
Option B (callout inside a @testSetup method) — setup methods create data; a callout there runs in the same context as the DML it follows.
Option C (both after Test.startTest()) — the DML is inside the block with the callout, which is the situation the error describes.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_classes_restful_http_testing_dml.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_callouts_timeouts.htm

corrected.note: Answer D stands. The explanation claimed Test.startTest 'ensures that the DML operations are committed', which is false — no DML is committed in a test — and stated the restriction backwards as 'all callouts are made before any DML operations in a transaction'. The guide's rule is that the callout goes inside Test.startTest/Test.stopTest while the DML stays outside it.

question: A company uses Opportunities to track sales to their customers and their org has millions of Opportunities. They want to begin to track revenue over time through a related Revenue object. As part of their initial implementation, they want to perform a one-time seeding of their data by automatically creating and populating Revenue records for Opportunities, based on complex logic. They estimate that roughly 100,000 Opportunities will have Revenue records created and populated. What is the optimal way to automate this?
optionA: Use System.schedule() to schedule a Database.Schedulable class.
optionB: Use System.enqueueJob() to invoke a Queueable class.
optionC: Use Database.executeBatch() to invoke a Queueable class.
optionD: Use Database.executeBatch() to invoke a Database.Batchable class.
explanation:
Using Database.executeBatch() to invoke a Database.Batchable class is the optimal automation. A one-time pass over 100,000 Opportunities with complex per-record logic is what Batch Apex is for: the QueryLocator streams the Opportunities, each execute() chunk runs in its own transaction with fresh governor limits, and the whole job is monitored from Apex Jobs.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (System.schedule() with a Schedulable class) — scheduling gives a start time, not the chunked processing 100,000 records need; a scheduled job on its own runs under synchronous limits.
Option B (System.enqueueJob() with a Queueable) — a single transaction with a single set of limits; 100,000 records with complex logic will not fit.
Option C (Database.executeBatch() with a Queueable) — executeBatch takes a Database.Batchable; a Queueable does not compile there.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_batch_interface.htm

question:
A developer is developing a reusable Aura component that will reside on an sObject Lightning page with the following HTML snippet:
Hello!
 How can the component" controller get the context of the Lightning page that the sObject is on without requiring additional test coverage?
optionA: Add force:hasSobjectName to the implements attribute
optionB: Use the gerSubjectType method in an Apex class.
optionC: Set the sObject type as a component attribute.
optionD: Create a design attribute and configure via App Builder.
explanation:
Adding force:hasSobjectName to the implements attribute is how. The interface gives the component an sObjectName attribute holding the API name of the object whose record page it sits on, populated by the framework — so the controller reads v.sObjectName with no Apex and therefore no extra test coverage.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (a getSObjectType method in Apex) — adds Apex, which is precisely the test coverage the question wants to avoid.
Option C (set the sObject type as a component attribute) — someone has to populate it; the component would still not know its own context.
Option D (a design attribute set in App Builder) — pushes the job onto whoever configures each page, and is not the record context itself.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/lightning-component-reference/guide/force-has-sobject-name.html

question:
When the code is executed, the callout is unsuccessful and the following error appears within the Developer Console:
System.CalloutException: Unauthorized endpoint
Which recommended approach should the developer implement to resolve the callout exception?
optionA: Annotate the getERPCatalogContents method with @future(callout=true).
optionB: Change the access modifier for ERPCatalog from public to global.
optionC: Use the SetHeader() method to specify Basic Authentication.
optionD: Create a remote site setting configuration that includes the endpoint.
explanation:
Creating a remote site setting that includes the endpoint is the recommended resolution. "Unauthorized endpoint" means the org has not been told it may call that URL; Apex callouts are only permitted to domains registered under Remote Site Settings (or to a named credential), and registering the endpoint is what clears the exception.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (@future(callout=true)) — governs when a callout may run relative to DML; it does not authorise a destination.
Option B (change the class from public to global) — access modifiers have nothing to do with callout permissions.
Option C (setHeader() for Basic Authentication) — authenticates to the remote server; the error here comes from Salesforce refusing to send the request at all.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_callouts_remote_site_settings.htm

question: Which Salesforce feature allows a developer to see when a user last logged in to Salesforce if real-time notification is not required?
optionA: Calendar Events
optionB: Asynchronous Data Capture Events
optionC: Event Monitoring Log
optionD: Developer Log
explanation:
The Event Monitoring log is the feature. Login events are captured in the event log files, which are generated after the fact and can be queried or downloaded, so a developer can find when a user last logged in without any real-time notification being involved.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Calendar Events) — appointments and meetings; nothing to do with logins.
Option B (Asynchronous Data Capture Events) — not a Salesforce feature.
Option D (Developer Log) — debug logs capture Apex execution for a traced user; they are not a login history.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.real_time_event_monitoring_overview.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question:
A company has a custom component that allows users to search for records of a certain object type by invoking an Apex Controller that returns a list of results based on the user's input. When the search is completed, a searchComplete event is fired, with the results put in a results attribute of the event. The component is designed to be used within other components and may appear on a single page more than once.
What is the optimal code that should be added to fire the event when the search has completed?
explanation:
component.getEvent("searchComplete"), then evt.setParams({results: results}) and evt.fire() is the optimal code. searchComplete is a component event, retrieved from the component that registered it; its parameters are set with setParams(); and fire() dispatches it up the containment hierarchy to the parent that embedded this instance. Because a component event reaches only the containing component, each instance on the page communicates with its own parent and not with the others — which is why a component event rather than an application event is the right choice for a reusable search component.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B ($A.get("e.c:searchComplete") with evt.set("v.results", ...)) — application-event syntax for a component event, and set("v.results") tries to set a component attribute on an event object.
Option C (component.getEvent() with evt.set("v.results", ...)) — retrieves the event correctly but sets its parameter with the wrong method; event parameters go through setParams().
Option D ($A.get("e.c.searchComplete") with setParams) — application-event retrieval for a component event, and e.c.searchComplete uses a dot where the namespace separator is a colon.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.lightning.meta/lightning/events_component_fire.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.lightning.meta/lightning/events_component.htm

question:
A company has an Apex process that makes multiple extensive database operations and web service callouts.
The database processes and web services can take a long time to run and must be run sequentially.
How should the developer write this Apex code without running into governor limits and system limitations?
optionA: Use Queueable Apex to chain the jobs to run sequentially.
optionB: Use Apex Scheduler to schedule each process.
optionC: Use multiple structed methods for each process and callout.
optionD: Use Limits class to stop entire process once governor limits are reached.
explanation:
Using Queueable Apex to chain the jobs to run sequentially is how the developer should write it. Each queueable runs in its own transaction with its own governor limits, a job can make callouts, and enqueuing the next job from execute() guarantees the order — so a long sequence of heavy database work and web service calls proceeds one step at a time without any single transaction carrying all of it.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Apex Scheduler for each process) — scheduled jobs run at set times, not in a guaranteed sequence triggered by the previous step finishing, and scheduled Apex runs under synchronous limits.
Option C (multiple methods for each process and callout) — methods called in one transaction still share that transaction's limits.
Option D (the Limits class to stop the process) — detecting the limit does not avoid it; the work is simply abandoned part way.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_queueing_jobs.htm

optionA: Create a formula field to combine the createdDate and RecordType value, then filter based on the formula.
optionB: Break down the query into two individual queries and join the two result sets.
optionC: Annotate the method with the @Future annotation
optionD: Use the Database queryLocator method to retrieve the accounts.
explanation:
Breaking the query into two individual queries and joining the two result sets is the documented remedy. The Large Data Volumes best-practices guide names this exact case: if you use two indexed fields joined by an OR in the WHERE clause, the result set can exceed the index selectivity threshold, so decompose the query — run it as two queries and join the results. Each half then filters on a single indexed field and can use that index, and the union of the two result sets is the same set of Accounts the OR would have returned, which is what "preserving the entire result set" requires.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a formula field combining CreatedDate and RecordType) — a formula field over those inputs is evaluated at query time and a non-deterministic formula cannot be indexed, so the filter is no more selective.
Option C (@Future) — moves the same slow query into another transaction without making it any faster.
Option D (Database.getQueryLocator) — how Batch Apex streams a large result set; the same non-selective OR is still evaluated, so it addresses row limits rather than the performance problem.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_best_practices_soql_and_sosl.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/engineering/2013/07/maximizing-the-performance-of-force-com-soql-reports-and-list-views

corrected.note: Key B stands. The explanation argued for option D from its first line — 'Option D is correct because using the Database.QueryLocator method...' — while the key names B. The LDV best-practices guide settles it: two indexed fields joined by an OR can exceed the index threshold, and the stated remedy is to break the query into two queries and join the results.

question:
Universal Containers develops a Salesforce application that requires frequent interaction with an external REST API.
To avoid duplicating code and improve maintainability, how should they implement the APL integration for code reuse?
optionA: Use a separate Apex class for each API endpoint to encapsulate the integration logic.
optionB: Include the API integration code directly in each Apex class that requires it.
optionC: Create a reusable Apex class for the AFL integration and invoke it from the relevant Apex classes.
optionD: Store the API integration code as a static resource and reference it in each Apex class.
explanation:
Creating a reusable Apex class for the API integration and invoking it from the relevant Apex classes is how to implement it. One class owns the endpoint handling, request building, authentication and response parsing; every caller uses it, so a change to the API is made in one place and tested once.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a separate class per endpoint) — spreads the shared plumbing across many classes, duplicating exactly what should be common.
Option B (integration code inline in each class) — the duplication the question is trying to avoid.
Option D (integration code as a static resource) — static resources hold files for pages and components; Apex cannot execute code stored in one.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_callouts.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_classes_static.htm

question:
A developer wrote a trigger on Opportunity that will update a custom Last Sold Date field on the Opportunity's Account whenever an Opportunity is closed. In the test class for the trigger, the assertion to validate the Last Sold Date field fails.
What might be causing the failed assertion?
optionA: The test class has not defined an Account owner when inserting the test data.
optionB: The test class has not implemented SeeAllData=true in the test method.
optionC: The test class has not re-queried the Account record after updating the Opportunity.
optionD: The test class is not using System. runs () to run tests as a Salesforce administrator.
explanation:
The test class not having re-queried the Account record after updating the Opportunity is what might be causing it. The trigger updates the Account in the database, but the Account variable the test holds is the in-memory copy from before the Opportunity was closed; asserting on that copy sees the old Last Sold Date. The test must query the Account again after the update and assert on the fresh row.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (no Account owner defined) — the owner defaults to the running user; it has no bearing on a date field the trigger sets.
Option B (SeeAllData=true) — the Account and Opportunity were created by the test and are already visible to it.
Option D (System.runAs() as an administrator) — the running user already has the access to insert and update these records; permissions are not the failure.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_testing_best_practices.htm

optionA: Add a new method in the Apex controller class to retrieve the mailing addresses separately and modify the Lightning web component to invoke this method.
optionB: Extend the lightning-datatable component in the Lightning web component to include a column for the MailingAddress field.
optionC: Modify the SOQL query in the getAccountContacts method to include the MailingAddress field.
optionD: Modify the SOQL query in the getAccountContacts method to include the MailingAddress field and update the columns attribute in javascript file to add Mailing address fields.
explanation:
Modifying the SOQL query to include the MailingAddress field and updating the columns attribute in the JavaScript file is the change. The datatable renders only the columns it is configured with, from the data it is given, so both halves are needed: the query must return the address and the columns array must have an entry for it.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a separate method to retrieve the addresses) — a second round trip for a field the existing query can return in the same row.
Option B (extend lightning-datatable to add a column) — no extension is needed; columns are configuration passed to the component.
Option C (modify the query only) — the address comes back from Apex, but with no column configured the table never shows it.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/lightning-component-reference/guide/lightning-datatable.html

A public static Boolean firstRun flag on CaseTriggerHandler is the modification that fixes it. A static variable in Apex holds its value for the life of the transaction, so a static Boolean that is set once and checked before doing the work is the standard way to stop a handler from running a second time when something later in the same transaction updates the record again. That is the only mechanism among these options that survives past a single invocation.
Two caveats about this item as printed. Option A adds the static flag to the handler but never tests it, so read literally the code still runs on every invocation; what the answer is really identifying is the mechanism, not the snippet. And options B and D pass Trigger.newMap to a method whose parameter is List<Case>, which would not compile.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (trigger sets firstRun = true then tests it) — puts the flag in the right place but assigns firstRun = true at the top of the trigger, resetting the guard immediately before testing it.
Option C (instance Boolean in the handler) — an instance variable isn't visible from a static method and would be re-initialised with every new instance in any case.
Option D (local Boolean in the trigger) — re-created, and reset to true, each time the trigger fires.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_classes_static.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_triggers_bestpract.htm

corrected.note: Key A stands as the only option using the right mechanism — a static variable retains its value for the duration of the transaction, which is what makes it usable as a recursion guard. Flagged as defective: option A declares the static flag without ever checking it, so the printed code would not by itself prevent the second run, and options B and D pass a Map to a method that takes a List.

question:
A company has a web page that needs to get Account record information, such as name, website, and employee number. The Salesforce record 1D is known to the web page and it uses JavaScript to retrieve the account information.
Which method of integration is optimal?
optionA: Apex SOAP web service
optionB: SOAP API
optionC: Apex REST web service
optionD: REST API
explanation:
The REST API is the optimal integration. The page already knows the record id, so a single HTTP GET to the standard sobjects endpoint returns the Account's fields as JSON, which JavaScript consumes directly — no custom Apex to write, deploy or test.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Apex SOAP web service) — custom Apex plus XML for a retrieval the standard API already provides.
Option B (SOAP API) — standard, but XML-based and heavier for a browser script than a REST GET returning JSON.
Option C (Apex REST web service) — custom code for something the standard REST API does with no code at all.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_rest.meta/api_rest/intro_what_is_rest_api.htm

question:
A user receives the generic "An internal server error has occurred" while interacting with a custom Lightning component.
What should the developer do to ensure a more meaningful message?
optionA: Add an onerror event handler to the tag.
optionB: Add an error-view component to the markup.
optionC: Use platform events to process the error
optionD: Use an AuraHandledexception in a try-catch block.
explanation:
Using an AuraHandledException in a try-catch block is what the developer should do. When the Apex controller catches an error and throws System.AuraHandledException with a message of its choosing, that message replaces the generic "An internal server error has occurred" in what the component receives, so the component can show the user something meaningful.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (an onerror event handler on the tag) — a handler can react to the error, but the message it receives is still the generic one unless the server throws something better.
Option B (an error-view component) — no such base component exists.
Option C (platform events to process the error) — an event bus for notifying subscribers; it does not change the message returned to the calling component.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.lightning.meta/lightning/controllers_server_apex_custom_errors.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/lwc/guide/apex-error-handling.html

optionA:
Add the following code above record;
@wire(getRecord, { recordId: ‘$recordId’, fields: ‘$fields’ })
optionD:
Add the following code above record;
@api(getRecord, { recordId: ‘$recordId’, fields: ‘$fields’ })
explanation:
Adding @wire(getRecord, { recordId: '$recordId', fields: '$fields' }) above the record property is what must be done. getRecord from lightning/uiRecordApi is a wire adapter, so it is invoked with the @wire decorator, and the $ prefix makes both parameters reactive — the wire re-runs whenever recordId or fields changes, and the result lands in record.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (@wire with recordId only, fields read in renderedCallback) — getRecord requires fields (or layoutTypes) to know what to fetch, and renderedCallback is for post-render DOM work, not for assigning wired data.
Option C (@api(getRecord, ...)) — @api marks a public property; it is not how a wire adapter is invoked.
Option D (@api(getRecord, { recordId, fields })) — the same misuse of @api, with the right parameters on the wrong decorator.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/lwc/guide/reference-lightning-ui-api-record.html
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/lwc/guide/data-wire-service-about.html

question:
A page throws an 'Attempt to dereference a null object' error for a Contact.
What change in the controller will fix the error?
optionA: Declare a static final Contact at the top of the controller.
optionB: Use a condition in the getter to return a new Contact if it is null.
optionC: Change the setter's signature to return a Contact.
optionD: Change the getter's signature to be static Contact.
explanation:
Using a condition in the getter to return a new Contact if it is null is the change. The page binds to fields on the controller's Contact property, and if the property has never been set the page dereferences null; a getter that lazily instantiates the Contact guarantees there is always an object to bind to.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a static final Contact) — a constant reference that is never assigned the record the page needs, and static state does not belong to a page instance.
Option C (a setter that returns a Contact) — a setter's job is to store the value; its return type does not affect whether the property is null.
Option D (a static getter) — makes the getter a class-level method with no relationship to the page's instance data, and still returns null if nothing set it.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.pages.meta/pages/pages_controller_methods.htm

question:
A developer is tasked with creating a Lightning web component that is responsive on various devices, Which two components should help accomplish this goal?
Choose 2 answers.
optionA: lightning-navigation
optionB: Lightning-input-location
optionC: Lightning-layout
optionD: lightning-layout--item
explanation:
lightning-layout and lightning-layout-item are the two components. Together they form the responsive 12-column grid: lightning-layout is the container and each lightning-layout-item declares its width per breakpoint with size, small-device-size, medium-device-size and large-device-size, so the same markup reflows on a phone, a tablet and a desktop.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (lightning-navigation) — a service component for navigating to pages and records; it lays nothing out.
Option B (lightning-input-location) — an input for a latitude and longitude pair.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/lightning-component-reference/guide/lightning-layout.html
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/lightning-component-reference/guide/lightning-layout-item.html

question: A developer created a JavaScript library that simplifies the development of repetitive tasks and features and uploaded the library as a static resource called jsUtils in Salesforce. Another developer is coding a new Lightning web component (LWC) and wants to leverage the library. Which statement properly loads the static resource within the LWC?
optionA: import jsUtilities from '@salesforce/resourceUrl/jsUtils';
optionB: <lightning-require scripts="{!$Resource.jsUtils}"/>
optionC: const jsUtility = $A.get('$Resource.jsUtils');
optionD: import { jsUtilities } from '@salesforce/resourceUrl/jsUtils';
explanation:
import jsUtilities from '@salesforce/resourceUrl/jsUtils'; is the statement. Static resources are loaded into a Lightning web component with a default import from the @salesforce/resourceUrl module, naming the resource after the final slash; Salesforce's guide gives the form directly as import myLib from "@salesforce/resourceUrl/myLib";. The imported value is the resource's URL, which you then hand to loadScript or loadStyle from lightning/platformResourceLoader.
All four options and the stem reached this deck with OCR damage from the scrape and have been repaired against the documented syntax; the answer is unchanged.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (<lightning-require scripts="{!$Resource.jsUtils}"/>) — Aura's ltng:require with a $Resource expression; neither exists in a Lightning web component.
Option C ($A.get('$Resource.jsUtils')) — $A is the Aura framework's global; it means nothing inside LWC.
Option D (import { jsUtilities } from ...) — the right module imported as a named export; @salesforce/resourceUrl/<name> exposes only a default export, so the braces are exactly what makes it wrong.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/lwc/guide/create-resources.html
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/lwc/guide/js-third-party-library.html

question:
Just prior to a new deployment the Salesforce administrator, who configured a new order fulfillment process feature in a developer sandbox, suddenly left the company.
Ag part of the UAT cycle, the users had fully tested all of the changes in the sandbox and signed off on them; making the Order fulfillment feature ready for its go-live in the production environment.
Unfortunately, although a Change Set was started, it was not completed by the former administrator.
A developer is brought in to finish the deployment.
What should the developer do to identify the configuration changes that need to be moved into production?
optionA: In Salesforce setup, look at the last modified date for every object to determine which should be added to the Change Set.
optionB: Use the Metadata API and a supported development IDE to push all of the configuration from the sandbox into production to ensure no changes are lost.
optionC: Leverage the Setup Audit Trail to review the changes made by the departed Administrator and identify which changes should be added to the Change Set.
optionD: Set up Continuous Integration and a Git repository to automatically merge all changes from the sandbox metadata with the production metadata.
explanation:
Leveraging the Setup Audit Trail to review the changes made by the departed administrator is what the developer should do. The audit trail lists every Setup change for the last 180 days with the date, the user and what changed, so filtering it to the former administrator's entries gives the precise list of components to add to the Change Set.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (check every object's last-modified date) — misses changes that are not objects (flows, permission sets, page layouts) and cannot tell the administrator's changes from anyone else's.
Option B (push all configuration from the sandbox with the Metadata API) — deploys everything, including untested work and sandbox-only settings, rather than the signed-off feature.
Option D (set up CI and a Git repository) — a sound long-term practice, but it does not identify which of the existing sandbox changes belong to this feature.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.admin_monitorsetup.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question:
For compliance purposes, a company is required to track long-term product usage in their org. The information that they need to log will be collected from more than one object and, over time, they predict they will have hundreds of millions of records.
What should a developer use to implement this?
optionA: Setup audit trail
optionB: Field audit trail
optionC: Big objects
optionD: Field history tracking
explanation:
Big objects are what the developer should use. They are built for hundreds of millions of records that must be retained but rarely change, they can hold data gathered from several objects, and they do not count against regular data storage — which is the compliance-archive shape described.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Setup audit trail) — records configuration changes in Setup, not product usage.
Option B (Field audit trail) — retains field history for up to ten years, but only for changes to tracked fields on a single object, not usage data assembled from many.
Option D (Field history tracking) — the same limitation with a far shorter retention period.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.bigobjects.meta/bigobjects/big_object.htm

question:
A company has reference data stored in multiple custom metadata records that represent default information and delete behavior for certain geographic regions.
When a contact is inserted, the default information should be set on the contact from the custom metadata records based on the contact's address information.
Additionally, if a user attempts to delete a contact that belongs to a flagged region, the user must get an error message.
Depending on company personnel resources, what are two ways to automate this?
Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Remote action
optionB: Flow Builder
optionC: Apex trigger
optionD: Apex invocable method
explanation:
Flow Builder and an Apex trigger are the two ways. A record-triggered flow can read the custom metadata, set the defaults on a Contact before it is saved, and — on a delete-triggered flow — raise a custom error to block the deletion; an Apex trigger does the same with before insert and before delete handlers and addError(). Which one fits depends on whether the team has developers, which is what "depending on company personnel resources" is pointing at.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (remote action) — a Visualforce JavaScript remoting mechanism; it does not run when a record is inserted or deleted.
Option D (Apex invocable method) — code that only runs when something calls it; on its own it automates nothing, and the flow that would call it is option B.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.flow_ref_elements_custom_error.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_triggers.htm

optionB: Add Test.startTest() before and Test.stopTest() after insert acct.
optionC: Add Test.startTest() before and Test.stopTest() after AuditUtil.incrementViewed.
optionD: Change the initialization to acct.Number_Of_Times_Viewed__c = 1.

The method is @future, so its DML runs asynchronously and is not visible when the test queries the Account; wrapping the call in Test.startTest() and Test.stopTest() forces the future method to complete synchronously when stopTest() is reached, so the query afterwards sees the incremented value.

Option B (startTest/stopTest around insert acct) — brackets the wrong statement; the future call is still outside the block and still pending at the assertion.

question: Given a list of Opportunity records named opportunityList, which code snippet is best for querying all Contacts of the Opportunity's Account?
explanation:
The snippet that collects the distinct Account ids into a Set and then runs one Account query with a Contacts subquery is the bulkified pattern. It walks the Opportunities once to gather the ids, then issues a single query against those Accounts — one query however long opportunityList is, and the Set keeps an Account shared by several Opportunities from being queried twice.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (AccountId IN :opportunityList.AccountId) — does not compile: opportunityList is a List, so opportunityList.AccountId is not a valid expression.
Option B (Account query inside the for loop) — a SOQL query per Opportunity, which is the standard way to hit the 100-query governor limit on a bulk update.
Option D (query Contacts by o.ContactId) — asks the wrong question: Opportunity's ContactId holds the single primary contact derived from the opportunity contact role and is frequently null, so it returns at most one Contact per Opportunity rather than every Contact on the Account.

question: The use of the transient keyword in Visualforce page controllers helps with which common performance issue?
optionA: Reduces load times
optionB: Improves page transfers
optionC: Reduces view state
optionD: Improves query performance
explanation:
Reducing view state is the issue it helps with. The transient keyword marks a controller variable as excluded from view state, so it is not serialised into the hidden form field on every request; a smaller view state stays under the 170 KB limit and costs less to serialise, encrypt and transfer on each postback.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (reduces load times) — a side effect of a smaller view state on postbacks, but transient does nothing for the initial load or the queries behind it.
Option B (improves page transfers) — not a Visualforce concept.
Option D (improves query performance) — queries run exactly as before; transient only changes what is kept between requests.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_visualforce_best_practices.meta/salesforce_visualforce_best_practices/pages_best_practices_perf_code_view_state.htm

optionA: Annotate the Apex method with @AuraEnabled.
optionB: Implement the with sharing keyword in the class declaration.
optionC: Implement the without sharing keyword in the class declaration.
optionD: Use the WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED clause within the SOQL query.
explanation:
Implementing the with sharing keyword, using the WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED clause in the query, and annotating the method with @AuraEnabled(cacheable=true) are the three changes, one for each thing the stem asks for, and each doing a genuinely different job.
@AuraEnabled(cacheable=true) is the "efficiently" half. It is also not optional for this component: the LWC guide says "to use @wire to call an Apex method, annotate the Apex method with @AuraEnabled(cacheable=true)", and repeats that "the method must be decorated with @AuraEnabled(cacheable=true)". The cacheable form is what lets the client-side Lightning Data Service cache answer a repeat request without a round trip.
with sharing is the record-level half of "preserving security". It enforces the running user's org-wide defaults, role hierarchy, sharing rules and manual or Apex shares, so the query stops returning Leads the user has no right to see.
WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED closes the gap with sharing leaves, and that gap is real: the LWC security guide states plainly that "the with sharing and without sharing keywords set record-level security. They don't enforce object-level and field-level security." Without a clause on the query, a user with no read access to AnnualRevenue still gets that field back.
One currency note that matters more than the letters. WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED is the clause of this item's era, and it still works, but Salesforce has moved on: the current Secure Apex Classes page no longer mentions it, teaching WITH USER_MODE (or Security.stripInaccessible for graceful degradation) instead. And from API version 67.0 Apex database operations run in user mode by default, while an @AuraEnabled class that declares no sharing keyword already gets an implicit with sharing. Salesforce still recommends declaring both explicitly "so that your code is easier to maintain across API versions", which is why this item's changes remain good practice rather than redundant.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (@AuraEnabled without a parameter) — @AuraEnabled(cacheable=true) is @AuraEnabled with a parameter; a method carries one annotation, not two, so A and E are the same change written twice, and A is the version that leaves the method callable only imperatively rather than by @wire.
Option C (without sharing) — the trap in the item: it deliberately bypasses the record-level enforcement that with sharing exists to add.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/lwc/guide/apex-wire-method.html
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_classes_keywords_sharing.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_security_sharing_rules.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_classes_enforce_usermode.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/lwc/guide/apex-security.html
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/lwc/guide/apex-result-caching.html
