question:
Universal Containers develops a Visualforce page that requires the inclusion of external JavaScript and CSS files. They want to ensure efficient loading and caching of the page.
Which feature should be utilized to achieve this goal?
optionA: ActionFunction
optionB: PageBlockTable
optionC: Static resources
optionD: RemoteAction
explanation:
Static resources are the feature. Uploading the JavaScript and CSS as a static resource — a single file or a zip archive holding a whole library — lets the page reference it with $Resource, and Salesforce serves it from its own cache with appropriate headers, so the files load once and are reused across requests.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (actionFunction) — invokes a controller action from JavaScript; it loads no files.
Option B (pageBlockTable) — renders a table of data.
Option D (RemoteAction) — exposes an Apex method to JavaScript remoting; again nothing to do with loading assets.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.pages.meta/pages/pages_resources.htm

optionA: System.QueryException: Too many DML Statement errors on Contact
optionB: System.QueryException: List has more than one row for Assignment on Account
optionC: System.LimitException: Too many SOQL Queries on Account
optionD: System.LimitException: Too many SOQL Queries on Contact
explanation:
System.QueryException: List has more than one row for assignment to SObject is the expected result. The loop contains a SOQL query inside it, so it runs once per Contact, and it fails on the very first iteration: the inner query has LIMIT 5 and five Accounts were created today, so it returns five rows, and assigning a multi-row result to a single Account variable throws the assignment exception. The SOQL-in-a-loop governor limit would be the next problem, but this exception is raised first.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Too many DML statements on Contact) — a LimitException, not a QueryException, and ten updates are nowhere near the 150-statement limit anyway.
Option C (Too many SOQL queries on Account) — the query limit trips at the 101st query; with ten Contacts the loop would issue ten, and it never reaches the second.
Option D (Too many SOQL queries on Contact) — the Contact query runs once, in the loop header.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/langCon_apex_SOQL_working_with_results.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_gov_limits.htm

question:
Salesforce users consistently receive a "Maximum trigger depth exceeded" error when saving an Account.
How can a developer fix this error?
optionA: Split the trigger logic into two separate triggers.
optionB: Convert the trigger to use the 3suzure annotation, and chain any subsequent trigger invocations to the Account object.
optionC: Modify the trigger to use the L=MultiThread=true annotation.
optionD: Use a helper class to set a Boolean to TRUE the first time a trigger is fired, and then modify the trigger to only fire when the Boolean is FALSE.
explanation:
Using a helper class to set a Boolean to TRUE the first time the trigger fires, and modifying the trigger to run only when the Boolean is FALSE, is the fix. "Maximum trigger depth exceeded" means the trigger is re-entering itself — an update it performs fires it again, and so on past the platform's depth limit; a static Boolean in a helper class persists for the transaction, so the second and later invocations see it set and skip the work.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (split the logic into two triggers) — both triggers still fire on every re-entry; the recursion is unchanged.
Option B (convert the trigger to @future and chain invocations) — a trigger cannot be annotated @future, and moving the update asynchronously still fires the trigger again in the new transaction.
Option C (a MultiThread=true annotation) — no such annotation exists.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_classes_static.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_triggers_bestpract.htm

question:
Universal Containers needs to integrate with several external systems. The process Is Initiated when a record Is created in Salesforce, The remote systems do not require Salesforce to wait for a response before continuing.
What is the recommended best solution to accomplish this?
optionA: Outbound message
optionB: PushTopic event
optionC: Platform event
optionD: Trigger with HTTP callout
explanation:
A platform event is the recommended solution. Publishing an event when the record is created is fire-and-forget — the transaction continues without waiting — and any number of external systems can subscribe to the same event over CometD or Pub/Sub API, with replay if a subscriber was offline, which is the shape of "several external systems" that "do not require Salesforce to wait".
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (outbound message) — asynchronous too, but each outbound message targets one SOAP endpoint, so several systems means several messages and workflow-era configuration; the event bus serves all subscribers from one publish.
Option B (PushTopic event) — the legacy streaming mechanism for record changes matched by a SOQL query, superseded by Change Data Capture and platform events, with tighter limits and no custom payload.
Option D (trigger with HTTP callout) — a synchronous callout is not allowed from a trigger, and a callout by nature waits for the response the requirement says is not needed.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.platform_events.meta/platform_events/platform_events_publish.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.platform_events.meta/platform_events/platform_events_subscribe.htm

optionA:
Account a = controller.getAccount('TestAccount');
System.assertEquals( 'TestAccount', a.Name );
optionD: Account a = MyRemoter.getAccount('TestAccount'); System.assertEquals( 'TestAccount', a.Name );
explanation:
Account a = MyRemoter.getAccount('TestAccount'); followed by the assertion is the snippet. getAccount is a static method, so it is called on the class, and @RemoteAction methods are required to be static, which is why none of the instance-based calls are right.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (controller.getAccount(...)) — refers to a controller variable the test never declares.
Option B (new MyRemoter() then remote.getAccount(...)) — reaches the static method through an instance; Apex tolerates that in places, but it is not how a static method is meant to be invoked and does not reflect how the remote action is called from the page.
Option C (new MyRemoter('TestAccount') then remote.getAccount()) — passes an argument to a constructor that takes none and then calls getAccount() without the argument it requires, so it would not compile.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.pages.meta/pages/pages_js_remoting.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_classes_static.htm

optionB: Use the browser's dev tools to debug the JavaScript.
optionC: Enable Debug Mode for Lightning components for the user.

console.log() messages, the browser's dev tools, and enabling Debug Mode for Lightning components are the three techniques. question:
A company wants to incorporate a third-party web service to set the Address fields when an Account is inserted, if they have not already been set.
What is the optimal way to achieve this?
optionA: Create a Workflow Rule, execute a Queueable job from it, and make a callout from the Queueable job.
optionB: Create an Apex trigger, execute a Queueable job from it, and make a callout from the Queueable job.
optionC: Create a Process, execute a Queueable job from it, and make a callout from the Queueable job.
optionD: Create a Before Save Flow, execute a Queueable job from it, and make a callout from the Queueable job.
explanation:
Creating an Apex trigger that executes a Queueable job, with the callout made from the Queueable, is the optimal way. A callout cannot be made synchronously from a trigger, so the trigger enqueues a job carrying the ids of the Accounts whose address is blank; the Queueable runs in its own transaction, makes the callout, and updates the Accounts with the result.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Workflow Rule executing a Queueable) — a workflow rule cannot run Apex.
Option C (a Process executing a Queueable) — Process Builder could call an invocable method that enqueued a job, but the tool is retired and adds a layer for nothing the trigger does not do directly.
Option D (a before-save Flow executing a Queueable) — before-save record-triggered flows cannot call Apex actions; only after-save flows can.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_queueing_jobs.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_callouts_timeouts.htm

question: How can a developer efficiently incorporate multiple JavaScript libraries in an Aura component?
optionA: Use JavaScript remoting and script tags.
optionB: Use CDNs with script attributes.
optionC: Implement the libraries in separate helper files.
optionD: Join multiple assets from a static resource.
explanation:
Joining multiple assets from a static resource is the efficient way. Several libraries are uploaded together as one zip static resource and loaded with a single ltng:require whose scripts attribute lists each file inside the archive; the framework loads them in the order given, once, and the archive is served from Salesforce's cache.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (JavaScript remoting and script tags) — remoting is a Visualforce mechanism for calling Apex, and raw script tags are not permitted in Aura markup.
Option B (CDNs with script attributes) — the Lightning Component framework's content security policy blocks scripts from external hosts; libraries must be static resources.
Option C (libraries in separate helper files) — a helper file holds the component's own functions; pasting a library into it defeats caching and makes it unmaintainable.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.lightning.meta/lightning/js_libs_platform.htm

question: Part of a custom Lightning Component displays the total number of Opportunities in the org, which is in the millions. The Lightning Component uses an Apex Controller to get the data it needs. What is the optimal way for a developer to get the total number of Opportunities for the Lightning Component?
optionA: Apex Batch job that counts the number of Opportunity records
optionB: SUM() SOQL aggregate query on the Opportunity object
optionC: SOQL for loop that counts the number of Opportunities records
optionD: COUNT() SOQL aggregate query on the Opportunity object
explanation:
A COUNT() SOQL aggregate query on the Opportunity object is the optimal way. COUNT() asks the database for a number rather than for records, and the Apex Developer Guide is precise about what that costs: for COUNT() and COUNT(fieldName), limits are counted as one query row — unless the query carries a GROUP BY, in which case one query row per grouping is consumed. So counting millions of Opportunities spends a single row against the 50,000-row query limit.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a batch job that counts the records) — asynchronous and far heavier than one query, for a number the component needs in order to render.
Option B (a SUM() aggregate query) — every aggregate function other than COUNT() and COUNT(fieldName) counts each row used by the aggregation as a query row, so SUM() over millions of Opportunities exceeds the 50,000-row limit outright — quite apart from totalling a currency field instead of counting records.
Option C (a SOQL for loop that counts) — retrieves the records it iterates, so it hits the same row limit.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.soql_sosl.meta/soql_sosl/sforce_api_calls_soql_select_count.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/langCon_apex_SOQL_agg_fns.htm

question: A company has a custom object, Order__c, that has a required, unique, external ID field called Order_Number__c. Which statement should be used to perform the DML necessary to insert new records and update existing records in a List of Order__c records?
optionA: upsert orders;
optionB: upsert orders Order_Number__c;
optionC: merge orders Order_Number__c;
optionD: merge orders;
explanation:
upsert orders Order_Number__c; is the statement. Naming the external ID field makes the upsert match incoming records on Order_Number__c: existing records with a matching value are updated and unmatched ones are inserted, all in one DML statement, with no need to know Salesforce ids.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (upsert orders;) — matches on the Salesforce record Id, which new records from an external system will not have, so everything is inserted and duplicates result.
Option C (merge orders Order_Number__c;) — merge combines duplicate Leads, Contacts or Accounts; it does not take an external ID and does not work on custom objects.
Option D (merge orders;) — the same wrong operation, with no matching field at all.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/langCon_apex_dml_examples_upsert.htm

optionA: System.LimitException: Too many future calls
optionB: System.LimitException: Too many callouts
optionC: System.LimitException: Too many SOQL queries
optionD: System.CalloutException: Callout from triggers are currently not supported
explanation:
System.LimitException: Too many future calls is the exception this code can trigger. The helper's notifyExternalSystem is a properly annotated @future(callout=true) method, so calling it from the trigger is allowed — but the trigger calls it once per record inside the loop over Trigger.new, and Execution Governors and Limits sets the maximum number of methods with the future annotation per Apex invocation at 50. A bulk update of more than 50 Accounts (a Data Loader batch is 200) therefore throws Too many future calls on the 51st iteration. Note that the stem asks which LimitException the code could trigger, and this is the only option that is one.
The bulk-safe shape is a single future call per transaction: collect the ids from Trigger.new into a Set and pass the whole set to one @future(callout=true) method (or a Queueable), which then makes its callouts inside the asynchronous transaction.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Too many callouts) — each future invocation is its own transaction and makes one callout, well under the 100-callout limit; the calls never share a transaction.
Option C (Too many SOQL queries) — the same: one query per future transaction, never 101 in one.
Option D (Callout from triggers are currently not supported) — a CalloutException, not a LimitException, and it is raised only when a callout is attempted synchronously in trigger context; here the callout is correctly deferred to a future method, so this error does not occur. This option was the key until 2026-09-11, on a reading of the scraped code in which the @future annotation appeared to be missing; the source's `AccountTriggerHelperfuture(callout=true) {` is the annotation with its line break, `{` and `@` lost in the scrape.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_callouts_timeouts.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_classes_annotation_future.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_gov_limits.htm

The trigger calls the future method once per record, so a bulk update throws Too many future calls. question: A developer is using a third-party JavaScript library to create a custom user interface in Visualforce. The developer needs to use JavaScript to get data from a controller method in response to a user action. How can the developer accomplish this?
optionA: Use <apex:actionFunction> to create a JavaScript wrapper for the controller method
optionB: Use the @RemoteAction annotation on the method definition with JavaScript Remoting
optionC: Use the $Controller global variable to access the controller method via JavaScript
optionD: Use <apex:actionSupport> to enable JavaScript support for the controller method
explanation:
Using the @RemoteAction annotation on the method with JavaScript Remoting is how. The method is declared global static and annotated @RemoteAction, and the page's JavaScript calls it with Visualforce.remoting.Manager.invokeAction (or the generated {!$RemoteAction...} wrapper), receiving the result in a callback — no form, no view state, no re-render, which is exactly what a third-party JavaScript UI needs.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (<apex:actionFunction>) — generates a JavaScript wrapper, but it must live inside an apex:form, submits view state, and returns by re-rendering page regions rather than handing data to a script.
Option C (a $Controller global variable) — does not exist.
Option D (<apex:actionSupport>) — attaches AJAX behaviour to a Visualforce component's browser event; it is not callable from arbitrary JavaScript.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.pages.meta/pages/pages_js_remoting.htm

optionA: A user is creating the record as Closed
optionB: workflow rule is firing with a Create Task action
optionC: A workflow rule is firing with a Field Update action
optionD: A user is editing the record multiple times
explanation:
A workflow rule firing with a Field Update action is what could cause it. A field update re-saves the record after the initial save, which fires the after-update trigger a second time in the same transaction; on that second pass Trigger.oldMap comes from the first save, where IsClosed was already true — but if the workflow runs on the same save that closed the Case, the re-fired trigger can still evaluate the closing condition and insert another Survey__c. The usual remedy is a static flag so the survey logic runs only once per transaction.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a user creating the record as Closed) — the isInsert branch fires once and creates one Survey.
Option B (a workflow rule with a Create Task action) — creating a Task does not re-save the Case, so the trigger does not re-fire.
Option D (a user editing the record multiple times) — on a later edit Trigger.oldMap shows IsClosed already true, so the condition is false and no Survey is added.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_triggers_bestpract.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_classes_static.htm

optionA: Use the asyncSend() method of the HTTP class to send the request in async context
optionB: Ensure all callouts are completed prior to executing DML statements
optionC: Move the web service callout into an @future method
optionD: Use Database.insert(order, true) to immediately commit any database changes
explanation:
Ensuring all callouts are completed prior to executing DML statements, or moving the web service callout into an @future method, are the two things the developer should do. The error occurs because the insert of the Order runs before the HTTP callout in the same transaction, and Salesforce forbids a callout while there is uncommitted DML. Reordering so the callout happens first removes the pending work; an @future(callout=true) method runs the callout in its own transaction after the current one commits.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (the asyncSend() method of the Http class) — no such method exists.
Option D (Database.insert(order, true) to commit immediately) — the second argument is allOrNone, not a commit flag; the DML is still pending when the callout runs, so the same error fires.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_callouts_timeouts.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_classes_annotation_future.htm

question: What is the transaction limit for the number of DML statements allowed?
optionC: 100 (synchronous), 200 (async)
optionD: 200 (synchronous), 100 (async)
explanation:
150 is the limit. Execution Governors and Limits sets the total number of DML statements issued per transaction at 150, and the figure is the same in synchronous and asynchronous contexts.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (20) — not a DML figure; no governor limit on DML is that small.
Option B (2,000) — not a governor limit; it is, for example, the maximum rows a SOSL query returns.
Option C (100 synchronous, 200 async) — those are the SOQL query limits, not DML.
Option D (200 synchronous, 100 async) — the SOQL figures reversed.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_gov_limits.htm

question: What is the transaction limit for the number of records per DML statement?
explanation:
10,000 is the number, and the precise wording matters: Execution Governors and Limits states it as the total number of records processed as a result of DML statements in a transaction, not an allowance per statement. Ten inserts of 1,000 records each exhaust it exactly as a single insert of 10,000 would, and records touched by cascading automation — triggers, flows, roll-up recalculations — count against the same total. That is why a mass update can fail on this limit even though no individual DML statement comes close to 10,000 rows.
The companion limit is 150 DML statements per transaction. Both are transaction-wide and both are the same in synchronous and asynchronous contexts.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (5,000) — not a DML limit.
Option B (20,000) — not a DML limit; it is, for instance, the number of records a report over an external object fetches.
Option C (50,000) — the limit on rows retrieved by SOQL queries, not on rows processed by DML.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_gov_limits.htm

corrected.note: Answer D (10,000) stands. The explanation described it as a per-statement ceiling — 'in a single DML operation you can process up to 10,000 records at once' — but the governor is the total number of records processed by DML across the whole transaction. The deck's own cascading-trigger question depends on the transaction-wide reading, so the two explanations contradicted each other.

question: What is the transaction limit on the max timeout for all callouts?
optionA: 120 seconds
optionB: 60 seconds
optionC: 120 seconds (synchronous); 200 seconds (async)
optionD: 60 seconds (synchronous); 200 seconds (async)
explanation:
120 seconds is the limit. The cumulative timeout for all callouts — HTTP and web service — in a single Apex transaction is 120 seconds, a total across every callout in the transaction, and it is the same in synchronous and asynchronous contexts.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (60 seconds) — not the cumulative limit; 60 seconds is, for example, the per-attempt timeout of an outbound message.
Option C (120 synchronous, 200 async) — the limit does not differ by context.
Option D (60 synchronous, 200 async) — neither figure is right.
Option E (no limit) — there is one, and a transaction that exceeds it fails.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_callouts_timeouts.htm

optionA: AccountControllerExt extension = new AccountControllerExt(acct);
optionB:
ApexPages.StandardController sc = new ApexPages.StandardController(acct.Id);
 AccountControllerExt extension = new AccountControllerExt(sc);
optionC:
ApexPages.StandardController sc = new ApexPages.StandardController(acct); 
AccountControllerExt extension = new AccountControllerExt(sc);
optionD: AccountControllerExt extension = new AccountControllerExt(acct.Id);
explanation:
Constructing an ApexPages.StandardController from the Account record and passing it to the extension's constructor is what should be added. A controller extension's constructor takes a StandardController, and the StandardController constructor takes the sObject itself — so new ApexPages.StandardController(acct) followed by new AccountControllerExt(sc) builds the extension exactly as the page would.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (new AccountControllerExt(acct)) — an extension is not constructed from an sObject; it needs a StandardController.
Option B (new ApexPages.StandardController(acct.Id)) — the StandardController constructor takes a record, not an Id.
Option D (new AccountControllerExt(acct.Id)) — the same problem as A, with an Id instead of a record.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.pages.meta/pages/apex_ApexPages_StandardController_ctor.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexref.meta/apexref/apex_pages_standardcontroller.htm

question: A developer created a new trigger that inserts a Task when a new Lead is created. After deploying to production, an outside integration is periodically reporting errors. Which change should the developer make to ensure the integration is not affected with minimal impact to business logic?
optionA: Remove the Apex Class from the Integration User's Profile.
optionB: Use the Database method with allOrNone set to False.
optionC: Use a Try/Catch block after the insert statement.
optionD: Deactivate the Trigger before the Integration runs.
explanation:
Using the Database method with allOrNone set to false is the change. Inserting the Tasks with Database.insert(tasks, false) inside the trigger lets an individual Task failure be reported in the SaveResult rather than thrown, so the Lead — and the integration that created it — still commits, while the Task logic keeps running for every record it can.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (remove the class from the integration user's profile) — Apex class access does not gate triggers, and skipping the logic for one user is not "minimal impact to business logic".
Option C (a try/catch after the insert) — catching the exception in a trigger still leaves the failed DML rolled back and the Lead insert failed unless the exception is handled record by record, which is what partial-success DML does for you.
Option D (deactivate the trigger before the integration runs) — turns the business logic off entirely.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexref.meta/apexref/apex_methods_system_database.htm

question:
An environment has two Apex Triggers: 
an after-update trigger on Account and an after-update trigger on Contact.
The Account after-update trigger fires whenever an Account's address is updated, and it updates every associated Contact with that address. 
The Contact after-update trigger fires on every edit, and it updates every Campaign Member record related to the Contact with the Contact's state. 
Consider the following: A mass update of 200 Account records' addresses, where each Account has 50 Contacts. Each Contact has 1 Campaign Member. This means there are 10,000 Contact records across the Accounts and 10,000 Campaign Member records across the contacts. What will happen when the mass update occurs?
optionA: The mass update will fail, since the two triggers fire in the same context, thus exceeding the number of records processed by DML statements.
optionB: There will be no error, since each trigger fires within its own context and each trigger does not exceed the limit of the number of records processed by DML statements.
optionC: There will be no error, since the limit on the number of records processed by DML statements is 50,000.
optionD: The mass update of Account address will succeed, but the Contact address updates will fail due to exceeding number of records processed by DML statements.
explanation:
The mass update will fail, since the two triggers fire in the same context and together exceed the number of records processed by DML statements. All cascading DML runs in a single transaction that shares the limit of 10,000 records processed by DML: the update of 200 Accounts cascades to 10,000 Contact updates, which cascade to 10,000 Campaign Member updates — roughly 20,200 records processed by DML in one transaction. The triggers do not each receive a fresh limit.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (each trigger has its own context) — a trigger fired by DML inside another trigger runs in the same transaction, under the same limits.
Option C (the limit is 50,000) — 50,000 is the SOQL row-retrieval limit; the DML limit is 10,000 records.
Option D (Accounts succeed, Contacts fail) — a governor limit exception rolls back the whole transaction, so the Account updates do not survive either.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_gov_limits.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_transaction.htm

question: A custom Visualforce controller calls the ApexPages.addMessage() method, but no messages are rendering on the page. Which component should be added to the Visualforce page to display the message?
optionA: <apex:message for="info"/>
optionB: <apex:facet name="messages" />
optionC: <apex:pageMessage severity="info" />
optionD: <apex:pageMessages />
explanation:
<apex:pageMessages /> is the component to add. It renders every message added to the page with ApexPages.addMessage(), with the standard severity styling, and is the general-purpose display for controller-raised messages.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (<apex:message for="info"/>) — shows the message for one specific component named in for; it does not show page-level messages.
Option B (<apex:facet name="messages" />) — a facet is a named slot inside another component; it is not a message display.
Option C (<apex:pageMessage severity="info" />) — displays a single hard-coded message you write in the markup, not messages from the controller.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.pages.meta/pages/pages_compref_pageMessages.htm

question: A developer is writing code that requires making callouts to an external web service. Which scenario necessitates that the callout be made in an @future method?
optionA: The callouts will be made in an Apex Trigger.
optionB: The callouts will be made in an Apex Test class.
optionC: The callout could take longer than 60 seconds to complete.
optionD: Over 10 callouts will be made in a single transaction.
explanation:
Callouts made in an Apex trigger is the scenario that necessitates an @future method. Triggers execute synchronously and cannot make synchronous callouts, so a callout invoked from trigger logic must be moved to an asynchronous @future(callout=true) (or Queueable) method.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (callouts in a test class) — tests cannot make real callouts at all; the answer there is a mock, not @future.
Option C (a callout longer than 60 seconds) — governed by the callout timeout and the 120-second cumulative limit; @future changes neither.
Option D (over 10 callouts in a transaction) — the limit is 100 callouts per transaction, and @future does not raise it.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_classes_annotation_future.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_callouts_timeouts.htm

question: Sometimes events on Salesforce need to be handled by an external system due to the scale or type of process being executed. Consider the use case of a user in Salesforce needing to get pricing for an order they are building in Salesforce while on the phone with a customer. The pricing logic already exists in a third-party system. Instead of recreating this logic in Salesforce, it will be leveraged by making a request of the third-party system. The response, in this case the pricing, will be returned and stored back in Salesforce. What is the optimal solution?
optionA: A Visualforce page that can make a real-time Apex callout to display and save the pricing back in Salesforce
optionB: An Apex trigger that upon saving the Order will make a real-time Apex callout, saving the pricing back in Salesforce
optionC: A Process Builder process and Outbound Message to fetch the pricing upon save and store the pricing in Salesforce
optionD: An ETL tool to process batches of newly saved Orders every few minutes to store the pricing back in Salesforce
explanation:
A Visualforce page that can make a real-time Apex callout to display and save the pricing back in Salesforce is the optimal solution. This is the Request and Reply pattern, which the integration patterns guide defines as Salesforce invoking a process on a remote system, waiting for that process to complete, and then tracking state based on the response. Every clause of the requirement matches: the rep is on the phone, the pricing has to come back during that interaction, and the returned price is stored on the record. The page's controller makes a synchronous Apex callout — the user acts, the controller calls the pricing service, and the response is displayed and saved in the same request.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (an Apex trigger making a real-time callout on save) — a callout from a trigger has to be made asynchronously, so the result cannot come back into the page the user is looking at, and it fires on save rather than while the order is being built.
Option C (Process Builder with an Outbound Message) — an outbound message is Fire and Forget: Salesforce hands the message off and does not wait for a reply, so nothing comes back to display.
Option D (an ETL tool every few minutes) — introduces minutes of delay, which is the opposite of what a live phone call needs.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/fundamentals/guide/integration-patterns.html
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_callouts.htm

question: A company represents their customers as Accounts that have an External ID field called Customer_Number__c. They have a custom Order (Order__c) object, with a Lookup to Account, to represent Orders that are placed in their external order management system (OMS). When an order is fulfilled in the OMS, a REST call to Salesforce should be made that creates an Order record in Salesforce and relates it to the proper Account. What is the optimal way to implement this?
optionA: Perform a REST GET on the Account and a REST POST to update the Order__c with the Account's record ID.
optionB: Perform a REST PATCH to upsert the Order__c and specify the Account's Customer_Number__c in it.
optionC: Perform a REST POST to update the Order__c and specify the Account's Customer_Number__c in it.
optionD: Perform a REST GET on the Account and a REST PATCH to upsert the Order__c with the Account's record ID.
explanation:
A REST PATCH to upsert the Order__c that specifies the Account's Customer_Number__c is the optimal implementation. The REST API's upsert is a PATCH to the sObject's external-id URL, and a lookup can be set by external id in the same body using the relationship name — for example "Account__r": { "Customer_Number__c": "CUST-12345" } — so one call creates the Order and relates it to the right Account without the caller ever knowing the Account's Salesforce id.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (GET the Account, then POST the Order with the record id) — two calls where one does the job, and the relationship-by-external-id syntax makes the lookup unnecessary.
Option C (a POST to update the Order__c with the Customer_Number__c) — POST creates a record; it cannot update one, and the option describes it as an update.
Option D (GET the Account, then PATCH the Order with the record id) — the right verb for upsert, but the extra GET is still an unnecessary round trip.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_rest.meta/api_rest/dome_upsert.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/langCon_apex_dml_nested_object.htm

question: What are three benefits of using static resources in Visualforce and Lightning Components? Choose three.
optionA: Static resource files are automatically minified.
optionB: Static resource files can be referenced by using the $Resource global variable instead of hardcoded IDs.
optionC: Static resource files can be packaged into a collection of related files in a zip or jar archive.
optionD: Static resource files do not count against an organization's quota of data storage.
optionE: Relative paths can be used in files in static resource archives to refer to other content within the archive.
explanation:
Referencing files with the $Resource global variable instead of hardcoded ids, packaging related files into a zip or jar archive, and using relative paths inside an archive are the three benefits, and the Visualforce guide names them as the reasons to prefer a static resource over uploading a file to the Documents tab: you can reference the resource by name with $Resource instead of hard-coding a document id, you can package a directory hierarchy of related files and upload it as a single .zip or .jar archive, and files inside an archive can refer to one another by relative path.
The storage option is a flaw in the item rather than a distractor, because it is also true. Salesforce's Data and File Storage Allocations page lists what counts toward file storage — attachments, Files home, CRM Content, Chatter files, the Documents tab, the File field on Knowledge articles, and Site.com assets — and then enumerates data storage object by object. Static resources appear in neither list. They carry their own separate allocation instead: 5 MB per resource and 250 MB per org. So four of the five statements here are correct while only three can be chosen; the three above are the ones the documentation frames as reasons to use the feature, which is what the question asks for.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (files are automatically minified) — a static resource is served as you uploaded it, so minified JavaScript has to be minified before upload.
Option D (do not count against data storage) — true, but not one of the documented reasons to use the feature; see the note above on why this item has four true statements.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.pages.meta/pages/pages_resources.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/lwc/guide/create-resources.html
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.overview_storage.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: Answer B,C,E stands as the three benefits the Visualforce guide itself lists, but the item is defective: option D is also true. Data and File Storage Allocations includes static resources in neither the file-storage list nor the data-storage list, and the Visualforce guide gives them a separate 5 MB per-resource / 250 MB per-org allocation, so they genuinely do not count against the data storage quota. This supersedes the earlier note, which had established only that the deck's original claim ("they do count against the org's file storage") was unsupported; the deeper check shows the opposite statement is the documented one.

question:
A company has a custom object, Sales Demo Request, that has a lookup to an Opportunity. It is required that a Sales Demo Request record be created when an

Opportunity's Probability is greater than 50%.

What is the optimal way to automate this?
optionA: Use an Apex Trigger on Opportunity.
optionB: Build a Flow on Opportunity.
optionC: Create a Workflow on Opportunity.
optionD: Build a Process on Opportunity.
explanation:
Building a Flow on Opportunity is the optimal automation. A record-triggered flow evaluates Probability on save and creates the related Sales Demo Request record declaratively, with no code to write, test or maintain.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (an Apex trigger) — code for a requirement the declarative tool covers outright.
Option C (a Workflow rule) — workflow actions are limited to field updates, tasks, email alerts and outbound messages; a workflow rule cannot create a custom object record.
Option D (a Process) — Process Builder could create the record, but it is retired in favour of Flow and new automation should not be built in it.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.flow_build_data_update.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=001096524&language=en_US&type=1

question: A company represents their customers as Accounts in Salesforce. All customers have a unique Customer_Number__c that is unique across all of the company's systems. They also have a custom Invoice__c object, with a Lookup to Account, to represent invoices that are sent out from their external system. This company wants to integrate invoice data back into Salesforce so Sales Reps can see when a customer is paying their bills on time. What is the optimal way to implement this?
optionA: Ensure Customer_Number__c is an External ID and that a custom field Invoice_Number__c is an External ID and Upsert invoice data nightly.
optionB: Query the Account Object upon each call to insert invoice data to fetch the Salesforce ID corresponding to the Customer Number on the invoice.
optionC: Create a cross-reference table in the custom invoicing system with the Salesforce Account ID of each Customer and insert invoice data nightly.
optionD: Use Salesforce Connect and external data objects to seamlessly import the invoice data into Salesforce without custom code.
explanation:
Ensuring Customer_Number__c is an External ID, adding an Invoice_Number__c External ID on Invoice__c, and upserting the invoice data nightly is the optimal implementation. The external ID on Account lets each invoice reference its Account by customer number — the upsert resolves the lookup without a query — and the external ID on Invoice__c makes the nightly load idempotent: new invoices insert, existing ones update, and re-running a load creates no duplicates.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (query the Account on each call for its Salesforce id) — an extra API call per invoice for a lookup the external-id reference resolves for free.
Option C (a cross-reference table of Salesforce ids in the invoicing system) — pushes Salesforce ids into the external system and creates a mapping that has to be maintained forever.
Option D (Salesforce Connect and external objects) — surfaces the data live from the external system rather than importing it; the requirement is to bring the invoice data into Salesforce.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_rest.meta/api_rest/dome_upsert.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_infrastructure_indexes.htm

question: In which of the following scenarios would it be acceptable to use programmatic sharing instead of declarative sharing? Choose three.
optionA: Every record created by sales users needs to be visible to their respective manager
optionB: Poor performance when using native sharing components
optionC: Team functionality is required on custom objects
optionD: There is an existing, external system of truth for user access assignments which will continue to drive access and be integrated with salesforce
optionE: You need to change record access to read/write for all users utilising a lightning component
explanation:
Poor performance with native sharing components, team functionality on custom objects, and an external system of truth for access assignments are the three acceptable scenarios. The governing principle is in Salesforce's platform sharing architecture guidance: Apex managed sharing, also called programmatic sharing, is for building sharing settings in code when a data access requirement can't be met by any other means.
Team functionality on custom objects qualifies, because account, opportunity, and case teams exist only on those standard objects — there is no declarative team feature to turn on for a custom object, so the share records have to be created in code. An external system that owns user access assignments qualifies too: declarative sharing is driven by ownership, role, and field criteria inside Salesforce, none of which can be driven by an outside system of record, so an integration writing share rows programmatically is the only route. Performance at scale is the softest of the three, and worth flagging as such: it is a real consideration — large volumes of sharing rules make group membership recalculation expensive — but it is a judgement about scale rather than a capability the declarative model lacks.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (every record visible to the creator's manager) — precisely what the role hierarchy does declaratively.
Option E (read/write for all users through a Lightning component) — an organization-wide default change, not a sharing design problem, and nothing to do with the component displaying the records.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/fundamentals/platform-sharing-architecture
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_bulk_sharing.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_bulk_sharing_understanding.htm

question: How long is field history retained?
optionA: 18 Months
optionB: 12 Months
optionC: 24 Months
optionD: 6 Months
explanation:
18 months is the retention. Standard field history tracking retains data for up to 18 months in the org, visible in the UI, and up to 24 months via the API; the commonly cited answer is 18 months. Longer retention requires the paid Field Audit Trail feature.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (12 months) — shorter than the documented window.
Option C (24 months) — the API-only window, not the retention period the platform documents for the org; it is the nearest distractor and the note above is why.
Option D (6 months) — not a documented figure.
Option E (36 months) — beyond standard retention; only Field Audit Trail reaches that far.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?language=en_US&id=sf.tracking_field_history.htm&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?language=en_US&id=sf.field_audit_trail.htm&type=5

question: Customer billing data must be added and updated into Salesforce from a remote system on weekly basis. Additionally, customer activity information must be extracted from Salesforce and put it into an on-premises data warehouse on a weekly basis. Which approach should be used to import data into Salesforce and export data out of Salesforce, taking into consideration that these imports and exports can interfere with end-user operations during business hours and involve large amounts of data?
optionA: Batch Apex, where Salesforce pushes data to and pulls data from the remote systems
optionB: Replication via third-party ETL to push data into Salesforce and pull data out in batches
optionC: Salesforce Connect to push data to and pull data from the remote systems
optionD: Call-in directly from each remote system to Salesforce APIs to push and pull the data
explanation:
Replication via a third-party ETL tool, pushing data into Salesforce and pulling it out in batches, is the approach. This is Batch Data Synchronization, which the integration patterns guide defines as data in Salesforce being created or refreshed to reflect updates from an external system, and changes from Salesforce being sent to an external system, with updates in either direction done in a batch manner. The requirement is bidirectional and weekly, which is that definition almost word for word. An ETL tool can be scheduled outside business hours so the load doesn't compete with users, it moves large volumes through the Bulk API, and it handles both directions with one tool.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Batch Apex pushing and pulling) — runs inside Salesforce and can push data out, but nothing about it pulls a weekly extract from a remote billing system on its own.
Option C (Salesforce Connect) — data virtualization: it reads external data live rather than replicating it, so the warehouse still doesn't get its copy.
Option D (each remote system calling Salesforce APIs directly) — can move the data but leaves you building and scheduling the orchestration for every system separately, which is what an ETL tool exists to avoid.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/fundamentals/guide/integration-patterns.html
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_asynch.meta/api_asynch/asynch_api_planning_guidelines.htm

question: Which scenario requires a developer to use an Apex callout instead of Outbound Messaging?
optionA: The target system uses a REST API.
optionB: The callout needs to be asynchronous.
optionC: The target system uses a SOAP API.
optionD: The callout needs to be invoked from a Workflow Rule.
explanation:
The target system using a REST API is the scenario that requires an Apex callout. Outbound Messaging delivers SOAP messages only, so a REST endpoint can be reached only from Apex — an HttpRequest built and sent in code.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (the callout needs to be asynchronous) — outbound messaging is asynchronous by design, with its own queue and retries.
Option C (the target uses a SOAP API) — exactly what outbound messaging handles.
Option D (invoked from a Workflow Rule) — a workflow rule can send an outbound message directly; it cannot run Apex.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.workflow_managing_outbound_messages.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_callouts.htm

question: As part of a new integration, a developer is asked to implement a new custom search functionality that is capable of performing unrestricted queries and can account for all values within a custom picklist field, Typec, on the Opportunity object. The search feature must also account for NULL values. The organization-wide default for the Opportunity object is set to Public Read-Only, and a new custom index has been created for the Typec field. There are more than 5 million Opportunity records within the environment, and a considerable amount of the existing records have NULL values for the picklist. Which technique should the developer implement to maximize performance when querying NULL values?
optionA: Use a SOSL query to return ALL opportunities that have a value of NULL in any field.
optionB: Use the OR operator to combine WHERE clauses to strictly search for each value within the picklist, including Typec = NULL.
optionC: Perform two SOQL queries; one to query Opportunities where Typec != NULL, and another to query where Type__c = NULL, then join the result set using Apex.
optionD: Create a formula field that substitutes NULL values for a string of text, create an index for the formula field, then use the formula within the WHERE clause.
explanation:
Creating a formula field that substitutes a string for NULL, indexing it, and filtering on that formula in the WHERE clause is the technique. A standard custom index does not help a query that filters on NULL, so the NULL half of the search stays non-selective against five million rows; a formula that turns NULL into a concrete value, with its own custom index, makes every value of the picklist — including the former NULLs — an indexed, selective filter.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a SOSL query for NULL in any field) — SOSL is text search; it cannot search for the absence of a value.
Option B (OR clauses for every picklist value including NULL) — an OR across many values, one of them NULL, is non-selective and falls back to a full scan.
Option C (two SOQL queries joined in Apex) — the query for Type__c = NULL is still the non-selective one, so splitting changes nothing.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_best_practices_soql_and_sosl.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_infrastructure_indexes.htm

question: As part of a custom interface, a developer team creates various new Lightning web components. Each of the components handles errors using toast messages. When the development is complete, all the components are added to the same Lightning page. During acceptance testing, users complain about the long chain of toast messages that display when errors occur loading the components. Which two techniques should the developer implement to improve the user experience? Choose two.
optionA: Use a [template] tag to display in-place error messages
optionB: Use public properties on each component to display the error messages
optionC: Use the window.alert() method to display the error messages.
optionD: Use a Lightning web component to aggregate and display all errors.
explanation:
Displaying in-place error messages with a conditional template tag, and using one Lightning web component to aggregate and display all errors, are the two techniques. Rendering each component's error inline with a template if:true block keeps the message where the failure is, and a single error-aggregating component on the page collects every error into one place — either way the user stops seeing a stack of toasts.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (public properties for the error messages) — exposing the message as an @api property changes nothing about how it is shown.
Option C (window.alert()) — a blocking browser dialog per error, which is worse than the toasts.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/lwc/guide/apex-error-handling.html
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/lwc/guide/create-conditional.html

optionA: import getOrders from '@salesforce/apex/OrderController.getAvailableOrders';
optionB: import getOrders from '@salesforce/apex/c.OrderController.getAvailableOrders';
optionC: import { LightningElement, api ) from 'lwc';
optionD: import { LightningElement, wire } from 'lwc';
explanation:
Importing getOrders from '@salesforce/apex/OrderController.getAvailableOrders' and importing wire from 'lwc' are the two changes. The Apex import must use the full @salesforce/apex/ module path, and because the code uses the @wire decorator, wire has to be imported from lwc; without either the component fails to compile.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B ('@salesforce/apex/c.OrderController...') — the module path does not take a namespace prefix for the default namespace.
Option C (import { LightningElement, api ) from 'lwc') — imports api, which the code does not use, and the mismatched bracket is itself a syntax error.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/lwc/guide/apex-wire-method.html
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/lwc/guide/reference-salesforce-modules

question: A developer has a Debug method within a class, which is invoked hundreds of times. What is the optimal functionality in the Developer Console to count the number of calls made to the method?
optionA: The "Execution Log" Panel
optionB: The "Execution Stack" Panel
optionC: The "Executed Units" tab under the Execution Overview
optionD: The "Execution Tree" tab under the Stack Tree Panel
explanation:
The "Executed Units" tab under the Execution Overview is the optimal functionality. It aggregates the log by unit — methods, queries, triggers — and shows how many times each ran and the time spent, so the count of calls to the Debug method is read straight off its row.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (the Execution Log panel) — the raw log lines; you would be counting entries by hand.
Option B (the Execution Stack panel) — the call stack at a selected point in the log, not a tally.
Option D (the Execution Tree tab) — the nested call tree, one node per invocation rather than a per-method count.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.code_dev_console_view_system_log.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: During the order of execution of a Visualforce page GET request, what happens after this step?
optionA: Evaluate constructors and expressions on custom components
optionB: Create view state if <apex: form> exists
optionC: Send the HTML response to the browser
optionD: Evaluate expressions, action attributes, and method calls
explanation:
Evaluating constructors and expressions on custom components is the step that follows. The documented order for a Visualforce get request is: the constructors on the custom controller or controller extensions run first; then any custom components on the page are created, their controllers' constructors run, and the expressions set on their attributes are evaluated; then assignTo attributes on those components execute; then page expressions, the action attribute on <apex:page>, and all other getter and setter calls are evaluated; then the view state is created if the page contains an <apex:form>; and finally the resulting HTML is sent to the browser.
This item is defective as scraped: the step the question asks you to look past — "after this step" — was carried by a diagram that did not survive, so the question cannot be answered from the printed text alone. Treat it as a prompt to know the sequence above.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (create view state if <apex:form> exists) — the second-to-last step, after the page expressions.
Option C (send the HTML response) — the final step.
Option D (evaluate expressions, action attributes and method calls) — the page-level evaluation, which comes after the custom components have been constructed.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.pages.meta/pages/pages_controller_get_request.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.pages.meta/pages/pages_controller_lifecycle.htm

corrected.note: Key A stands, but the explanation gave the order backwards — it said custom-component constructors are evaluated after the page's expressions, action attributes, and method calls, while the Visualforce guide places them before. Also flagged: the stem refers to 'this step' from a diagram lost in scraping, so the item is unanswerable as printed.

question: A developer needs to create a service that will process an email sent to it and create an account and contact using the contents of the email as data for the records. How might a developer accomplish this requirement?
optionA: Use the Apex Inbound Email Handler
optionB: Use the Fuel API with Email Data Extensions
optionC: Use Heroku Data Clips to Process Email
optionD: Use Auto-launched Flow and Process Builder
explanation:
Using the Apex Inbound Email Handler is how. An Apex class implementing Messaging.InboundEmailHandler, registered as an email service, receives each inbound email as a Messaging.InboundEmail object; the handler parses the subject, body and attachments and inserts the Account and Contact from that data.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (the Fuel API with Email Data Extensions) — Marketing Cloud's API for sending and data extensions; it does not receive email into the core platform.
Option C (Heroku Data Clips) — read-only SQL queries over Heroku Postgres.
Option D (an auto-launched Flow and Process Builder) — neither can receive an inbound email; something has to hand them the data first.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_classes_email_inbound.htm

question: How can Apex be used with Visual Workflow?
optionA: To set the version of a Flow being run
optionB: To start a Flow automatically
optionC: To add custom styling to a Flow
optionD: To control access to a Flow
explanation:
Starting a Flow automatically is how Apex can be used with it. The Flow.Interview class creates and starts a flow interview from code — Flow.Interview.createInterview(name, inputs).start() — so a trigger or a controller can launch a flow with no user involvement.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (set the version of a Flow being run) — Apex runs the active version; there is no API to pick another.
Option C (add custom styling) — a flow's look is set in Flow Builder and the screen components it uses, not by Apex.
Option D (control access to a Flow) — flow access is governed by profiles and permission sets.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexref.meta/apexref/flow_interview_class.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexref.meta/apexref/apex_namespace_Flow.htm

question: An integration user makes a successful login() call via the SOAP API.What can be used in the SOAP header to provide server authorization for subsequent API requests?
optionA: Named Credentials
optionB: Session ID
optionC: OAuth access token
optionD: Security token
explanation:
The Session ID is what goes in the SOAP header. A successful login() call returns a session id, and every subsequent SOAP API request carries it in the SessionHeader, which is how the server authorises the call.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Named Credentials) — a Setup feature for authenticating Apex callouts out of Salesforce; it plays no part in a SOAP client's headers.
Option C (an OAuth access token) — the credential of an OAuth flow; a login() call is the username-password SOAP flow, which yields a session id instead.
Option D (the security token) — appended to the password in the login() call itself, not sent on later requests.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api.meta/api/sforce_api_header_sessionheader.htm

question: A developer is creating unit tests for code that makes SOAP web service callouts. The developer needs to insert some test data as a part of the unit tests setup. What are three actions to enable this functionality? Choose three.
optionA: Surround the callout with Test.startTest(), Test.stopTest()
optionB: Surround the data insertion with Test.startTest(), Test.stopTest()
optionC: Implement the WebServiceMock interface
optionD: Update code to call Test.setMock()
explanation:
Surrounding the callout with Test.startTest() and Test.stopTest(), implementing the WebServiceMock interface, and calling Test.setMock() are the three actions. For a SOAP callout the mock is the WebServiceMock interface, registered with Test.setMock(WebServiceMock.class, new MyMock()), and the callout itself goes inside Test.startTest() and Test.stopTest() so the test data inserted beforehand does not count as pending DML when the callout runs. Note that Test.startTest() does not commit anything: nothing in a test is ever committed. It opens a fresh context with its own set of governor limits, and that is the boundary the callout restriction is measured against.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (surround the data insertion with startTest/stopTest) — the DML belongs outside the block; enclosing the callout, not the insert, is what allows both in one test method.
Option E (implement HttpCalloutMock) — the equivalent for HTTP and REST callouts, not for a class generated from a WSDL.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_callouts_wsdl2apex_testing.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexref.meta/apexref/apex_interface_webservicemock.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_classes_restful_http_testing_dml.htm

corrected.note: Answer A,C,D stands. The explanation asserted that wrapping the callout in Test.startTest()/Test.stopTest() means the data inserted beforehand 'is committed', which is false — a test never commits DML. Rewritten to say what the boundary actually does, and to state why HttpCalloutMock is the wrong interface for a WSDL-generated SOAP callout.

question: A developer has written an After Update trigger on Account. A workflow rule and field update cause the trigger to repeatedly update the Account records. How should the developer handle the recursive trigger?
optionA: Deactivate the trigger and move the logic into a Process or Flow
optionB: Deactivate the workflow rule to prevent the field update from executing
optionC: Use a static variable to prevent the trigger from executing more than once
optionD: Use a global variable to prevent the trigger from executing more than once
explanation:
Using a static variable to prevent the trigger from executing more than once is how to handle it. A static Boolean in a helper class keeps its value for the whole transaction, so the trigger sets it on its first run and checks it on every re-entry — the workflow field update's re-save fires the trigger again, sees the flag, and does nothing.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (deactivate the trigger and move the logic to a Process or Flow) — removes working logic to dodge a recursion that a one-line guard fixes.
Option B (deactivate the workflow rule) — removes the field update the business presumably still needs.
Option D (a global variable) — Apex has no global variables; global is an access modifier, and an instance variable is recreated on every invocation.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_classes_static.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_triggers_bestpract.htm

question:
A developer has a page with two extensions overriding the Standard controller for Case.

```html
<apex:page standardController="Case" extension="CaseExtensionOne,CaseExtension Two" showHeader="false">
```

Each extension has a method called Save. The page has a command button as defined:

```html
<apex:commandButton value="Save" action="{!save}"/>
```
optionA: All of the three Save methods will be executed
optionB: Save from Case Standard Controller will be executed
optionC: Save from CaseExtensionTwo will be executed
optionD: Save from CaseExtensionOne will be executed
explanation:
Save from CaseExtensionOne will be executed. With more than one extension on the same standard controller, a method defined in several places resolves to the leftmost extension — the one that appears first in the comma-separated extensions list. The Visualforce guide states this and gives the same shape of example: with extensions="ExtOne,ExtTwo" and getFoo() defined in both, the rendered value comes from ExtOne.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (all three Save methods run) — an override replaces the method; the others are never called.
Option B (the standard controller's Save runs) — any extension method with the same name takes precedence over the standard controller's.
Option C (Save from CaseExtensionTwo runs) — the second extension in the list loses to the first.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.pages.meta/pages/pages_controller_extension.htm

question: Choose the correct definition for <apex:actionSupport>.
optionA: Allows for controller methods to be called directly from Javascript. Must be encapsulated in <apex:form> tags. Unlike actionSupport, these function<apex:actionPoller>s can be called directly from Javascript code
optionB: Sends an AJAX request according to the time interval you specify. If this ever gets re-rendered, it resets
optionC: Adds AJAX support to another component (e.g. onClick, onMouseUp, onFocus, etc.)
optionD: Can be associated with an AJAX request (actionFunction/actionSupport/actionPoller) and shows content conditionally depending on the status of the request (in progress/complete). Use the "id" field to specify name; use "status" field on related components to connect them
optionE: Signifies which components should be processed by the server when an AJAX request is generated
explanation:
Adds AJAX support to another component, for events such as onclick, onmouseup and onfocus — that is the definition of <apex:actionSupport>. It attaches to a sibling component's browser event and invokes a controller action in response, re-rendering the regions named in reRender.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (controller methods callable directly from JavaScript) — describes <apex:actionFunction>.
Option B (an AJAX request on a time interval) — describes <apex:actionPoller>.
Option D (shows content depending on the status of a request) — describes <apex:actionStatus>.
Option E (which components the server processes on an AJAX request) — describes <apex:actionRegion>.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.pages.meta/pages/pages_compref_actionSupport.htm

question: Choose the correct definition for <apex:messages>.
optionA: Standard Salesforce formatting, throws a specific message on a page
optionB: Standard Salesforce formatting, shows all errors that occur on page. Can add more messages through the "ApexPages.addMessage" function
optionC: single message, without formatting, that can be associated with a specific component on the page
optionD: No formatting; displays all errors on a page
explanation:
Standard Salesforce formatting, showing all errors that occur on the page, with more messages addable through ApexPages.addMessage — that is the definition of <apex:messages>. It renders every page-level message, including those the controller adds.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a specific message thrown on a page) — describes <apex:pageMessage>, a single message written in the markup.
Option C (a single unformatted message tied to a component) — describes <apex:message>.
Option D (no formatting, all errors) — no Visualforce component matches; <apex:messages> applies standard formatting.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.pages.meta/pages/pages_compref_messages.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.pages.meta/pages/pages_compref_pageMessages.htm

question: Which of the following standard fields are indexed? Choose three.
optionA: Name
optionB: CreatedBy
optionC: SystemModStamp
optionD: LastModifedDdate
explanation:
Name, SystemModStamp and RecordType are the three indexed fields. Salesforce maintains indexes on a documented set of standard fields: RecordTypeId, Division, CreatedDate, Systemmodstamp, Name, Email (on contacts and leads), lookup and master-detail foreign keys, and the record Id, which is the primary key for every object. Of the choices, those three appear on that list without qualification.
One caveat about the remaining option. The Large Data Volumes guide writes that entry as "Systemmodstamp (LastModifiedDate)", treating the two as the same index rather than presenting LastModifiedDate as unindexed. So LastModifiedDate is not a clean distractor: this item works because the three fields named above are unambiguous, not because filtering on LastModifiedDate is documented to miss an index.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (CreatedBy) — not on the list; what carries the index is CreatedDate, the timestamp, not CreatedById.
Option D (LastModifiedDate) — documented alongside Systemmodstamp rather than as a separate index, which is why it is the weak distractor described above.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_infrastructure_indexes.htm

corrected.note: Answer A,C,E stands, but the explanation asserted that LastModifiedDate is not indexed. The LDV Indexes page lists the field as "Systemmodstamp (LastModifiedDate)", which implies the opposite. Rewritten to justify the three picks from what the list states outright, and to flag option D as an unreliable distractor rather than a documented negative.
